docs.title: 📱 Android Interview Prep (2026 Edition)
docs.text: Welcome to the ultimate preparation guide for Android Developers. This resource is designed to take you from Junior to Senior/Staff level by covering everything from core fundamentals to complex system design and CI/CD pipelines.

docs.title: 📱 Fundamentals
docs.text: Master the core building blocks of the Android OS. * Lifecycle: Deep dives into Activity and Fragment states. * Components: Services, Broadcast Receivers, and Content Providers. * Manifest & Context: Understanding the app's blueprint and memory-safe context usage.

docs.title: 🧠 Kotlin
docs.text: Modern Android is Kotlin-first. We cover language internals and idiomatic usage. * Core: Null safety, Extension functions, and Higher-order functions. * Advanced: Inline functions, Reified types, and Sealed Class hierarchies. * Asynchronous: Coroutines and Flow (StateFlow/SharedFlow).

docs.title: 🛠️ Jetpack Compose
docs.text: The declarative UI standard for Android. * State: remember, rememberSaveable, and State Hoisting. * Internals: Recomposition cycles and stability. * Effects: Managing side effects with LaunchedEffect and DisposableEffect.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architecture
docs.text: Design patterns that define professional, scalable apps. * Patterns: MVVM, MVI, and Clean Architecture. * DI: Hilt, Dagger2, and Koin. * Scalability: Modularization strategies and the Repository pattern.

docs.title: ⚡ Concurrency
docs.text: Efficient background processing. * Coroutines: Dispatchers, Scopes, and Structured Concurrency. * Flow vs LiveData: Migration strategies and use cases. * Threading: Handlers, Loopers, and the Main Thread.

docs.title: 🌐 Networking & Offline
docs.text: Data persistence and API communication. * Networking: Retrofit, OkHttp, and Interceptors. * Database: Room, Migrations, and Relationships. * Strategy: Offline-First Architecture and data synchronization.

docs.title: 🚀 Performance & Vitals
docs.text: Building "buttery smooth" experiences. * Optimization: Memory leaks (LeakCanary), ANRs, and App Startup time. * Metrics: App Vitals and Play Console performance tracking. * Debugging: Profilers, Logcat, and StrictMode.

docs.title: ⚙️ CI/CD & Release
docs.text: The "DevOps" of Android. * Pipelines: GitHub Actions and automated workflows. * Management: Release Strategies, App Bundles, and Gradual Rollouts.

docs.title: 🏗️ System Design
docs.text: Senior-level discussions on building complex systems. * Designing Image Loaders (Glide/Coil). * Real-time Chat and Feed systems. * Analytics and Logging SDKs.

docs.title: 🎓 Advanced & Security
docs.text: Going deep into the OS. * Internals: AOSP basics and Binder IPC. * Security: Keystore, ProGuard, and R8. * Form Factors: Foldables and Tablets.

docs.title: 🎯 Goal of This Project
docs.text: This project aims to create a practical Android interview preparation resource with: - Interview-Focused Answers: Not just documentation, but how to explain it to an interviewer. - 2026 Standards: Focused on Compose, KMP, and On-device AI. - Real Examples: Code snippets that actually work in production.

docs.title: Caching and pagination architecture
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Caching and Pagination Architecture Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Caching and pagination architecture determines perceived performance, data consistency, and backend load behavior. Policy clarity matters more than any single library choice.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• cache hierarchy (memory -> disk/db -> network)
  • freshness policy (TTL, version, etag)
  • pagination key strategy (page, cursor, token)
  • invalidation triggers (manual, time, mutation, server signals)

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation:
  • display paged state and load/error indicators
  • ViewModel/domain:
  • coordinate refresh/append intents
  • map cache/paging results to UI state
  • Data:
  • enforce cache policy and page merge logic

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. UI requests initial or next page.
  2. Repository checks cache validity.
  3. If needed, remote fetch runs with paging token.
  4. Data is merged/deduplicated and persisted.
  5. UI observes updated canonical paged state.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Key internals to define early:

  • canonical item identity and dedup rules
  • append/prepend retry behavior
  • refresh boundary and stale window policy
  • invalidation after writes that change list ordering

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
interface FeedPagingRepository {
    fun observeFeed(): Flow<List<FeedItem>>
    suspend fun refresh()
    suspend fun loadNextPage()
}

class FeedPagingPolicy(
    val staleAfterMs: Long,
    val pageSize: Int
)

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Where should pagination state live?
  • Cursor vs offset pagination tradeoffs?
  • How do you avoid duplicate items across pages?
  • What should invalidate cached pages?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• instrument cache hit rate and page load latency
  • backoff on repeated page fetch failures
  • protect against thundering-herd refresh behavior
  • validate paging under flaky network conditions

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • better UX latency and lower backend pressure
  • smoother long-list performance
  • Cons:
  • higher complexity in merge/invalidation logic
  • consistency edge cases under concurrent updates

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Staff-level answers should include operational metrics. A good architecture defines how teams measure cache effectiveness, page quality, and sync correctness over time.

docs.title: Clean architecture layering
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Clean Architecture organizes code by policy boundaries and dependency direction. The goal is long-term maintainability, not maximum layer count.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• inward dependency rule (outer depends on inner)
  • framework-independent business policy
  • stable interfaces at layer boundaries
  • explicit mapping between transport/domain/UI models

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation:
  • state rendering and user interaction handling
  • Domain:
  • business rules and use-case orchestration
  • Data:
  • infrastructure details (network, db, files, caches)

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. UI intent reaches ViewModel.
  2. ViewModel triggers use case.
  3. Use case calls domain repository interface.
  4. Data implementation executes integration work.
  5. Domain result returns and maps to UiState.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Keep domain contracts stable and place implementation churn in data modules.

Typical package/module split:

  • presentation (screen state + mappers)
  • domain (use cases + contracts)
  • data (adapters + source orchestration)

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
interface ProductRepository {
    suspend fun getProduct(id: String): Product
}

class GetProductUseCase(
    private val repository: ProductRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(id: String): Product = repository.getProduct(id)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Does every app need all three layers?
  • Where should model mapping live?
  • How do you avoid over-abstraction?
  • How does this impact build speed?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• introduce layers where complexity justifies them
  • keep boundary ownership explicit
  • codify dependency rules with lint/CI checks
  • track refactor friction as architecture health signal

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • clear boundaries and safer refactors
  • strong testing isolation
  • Cons:
  • more indirection and code overhead
  • potential boilerplate in simple features

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong candidates discuss pragmatic architecture: where strict layering was relaxed, what risks that introduced, and which guardrails kept the codebase healthy.

docs.title: Dagger and component graph
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Dagger and Component Graph Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Dagger gives fine-grained control over dependency graph architecture. It is powerful for complex systems but requires strong design discipline.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• component defines injectable graph boundary
  • subcomponent models child lifecycle scope
  • module provides/binds dependencies
  • compile-time validation catches wiring errors early

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Core platform modules:
  • provide shared infra services
  • Feature graph modules:
  • declare feature-specific implementations
  • Entry components:
  • expose required dependencies to Android boundary classes

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Root component initializes global graph.
  2. Child/subcomponent is created per feature or lifecycle scope.
  3. Requested object graph is resolved through providers/bindings.
  4. Injected classes execute domain/data flow.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Graph design decisions:

  • subcomponents vs component dependencies
  • multibinding for extensibility points
  • scope boundaries to prevent accidental object sharing

Complexity risks:

  • cyclic dependencies through bindings
  • over-centralized mega-modules
  • slow builds due to graph explosion

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Singleton
@Component(modules = [NetworkModule::class, RepositoryModule::class])
interface AppComponent {
    fun feedComponentFactory(): FeedComponent.Factory
}

@Subcomponent(modules = [FeedModule::class])
@FeatureScope
interface FeedComponent {
    @Subcomponent.Factory
    interface Factory {
        fun create(): FeedComponent
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When to use subcomponents vs component dependencies?
  • How do scopes map to Android lifecycles?
  • Why might Dagger builds become slow?
  • How do you debug missing binding chains?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• keep module ownership per team/feature
  • reduce public graph surface to essential contracts
  • fail PRs on unauthorized graph coupling
  • maintain graph diagrams for critical modules

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • maximal flexibility and explicit control
  • strong compile-time graph safety
  • Cons:
  • high setup/maintenance complexity
  • steeper onboarding and debugging costs

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Staff-level discussion should cover how graph governance evolves: ownership rules, build performance budgets, and strategies to prevent dependency sprawl.

docs.title: Dependency injection strategies
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Dependency injection is an architectural tool for explicit object graph design. At scale, DI quality affects reliability, testability, and developer velocity.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• constructor injection as default dependency declaration
  • interface-driven boundaries for replaceability
  • scope alignment with lifecycle to avoid leaks/churn
  • composition root controls graph assembly

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation:
  • request/use dependencies via constructors (ViewModel, coordinators)
  • Domain:
  • depend on interfaces for repositories/services
  • Data:
  • provide concrete implementations and adapters
  • Composition root (DI modules):
  • wire implementations to abstractions

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
DI itself is not data flow; it enables flow paths.

  1. App start creates root graph.
  2. Feature entry creates scoped dependencies.
  3. ViewModel receives use case and repository abstractions.
  4. Use case calls data implementations through interfaces.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Scoping decisions are architecture decisions:

  • app-wide singletons for stateless shared services
  • feature/session scopes for user-contextful components
  • ViewModel scope for screen state orchestrators

Mis-scoping patterns to avoid:

  • sharing mutable state as singleton unintentionally
  • recreating expensive clients per request path

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
class GetFeedUseCase(
    private val repository: FeedRepository
)

class FeedViewModel(
    private val getFeedUseCase: GetFeedUseCase
) : ViewModel()

@Module
@InstallIn(ViewModelComponent::class)
object FeedModule {
    @Provides
    fun provideGetFeedUseCase(repo: FeedRepository): GetFeedUseCase {
        return GetFeedUseCase(repo)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
  • How do you choose scope lifetimes?
  • When is a Service Locator acceptable?
  • How do you test graph-heavy code without brittle setup?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• standardize module/package conventions for bindings
  • keep binding ownership close to implementation modules
  • fail fast on missing/wrong bindings in CI
  • budget for annotation-processing build costs

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • explicit contracts and easier test doubles
  • consistent wiring patterns across large teams
  • Cons:
  • graph complexity and compile-time cost growth
  • steeper onboarding in very modular systems

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong senior answers discuss DI as socio-technical design: who owns bindings, how graph changes are reviewed, and how teams prevent dependency sprawl over time.

docs.title: Feature modules and boundaries
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Feature Modules and Boundaries Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Feature modules help scale product development when boundaries match user capability and team ownership. Good boundaries reduce coupling and release risk.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• feature-first module slicing by business capability
  • explicit inter-feature contracts
  • local ownership of UI/domain behavior
  • dependency direction toward shared contracts, not peer internals

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Feature module:
  • feature UI orchestration
  • feature-specific use cases and mappers
  • Shared/core modules:
  • common infra and cross-feature contracts
  • App shell:
  • top-level wiring and navigation composition

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Feature UI triggers feature use case.
  2. Use case calls local/shared contracts.
  3. Data is resolved by owning feature/data module.
  4. Result maps back into feature-local UI state.
  5. Cross-feature navigation/events use contract interfaces.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Boundary signals for healthy feature modules:

  • minimal imports from peer feature modules
  • API-only contract exposure
  • no direct access to peer internal models
  • isolated tests and build targets

Dynamic feature modules add delivery flexibility but operational complexity.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// contract module
interface ProfileEntry {
    fun open(userId: String)
}

// feature implementation module
class ProfileEntryImpl(
    private val nav: Navigator
) : ProfileEntry {
    override fun open(userId: String) = nav.go("profile/$userId")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How do you choose feature boundaries initially?
  • How do you prevent cross-feature dependency creep?
  • When are dynamic feature modules worth it?
  • How do you handle shared design-system dependencies?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• enforce dependency rules in CI
  • version and deprecate feature contracts explicitly
  • assign clear module ownership and on-call accountability
  • track build and integration cost per module

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • team autonomy and safer parallel delivery
  • more targeted releases and refactors
  • Cons:
  • contract coordination overhead
  • increased dependency management complexity

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior discussions should include boundary evolution. As product scope changes, feature boundaries should be revisited, not treated as permanent architecture law.

docs.title: Hilt in production
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Hilt standardizes dependency injection for Android lifecycle components. Its value is consistency and lower setup cost across teams.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• annotation-driven graph wiring
  • predefined component hierarchy
  • scope annotations tied to lifecycle
  • entry points for framework-created objects

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• App/platform layer:
  • define global bindings and singleton services
  • Feature layer:
  • declare feature-scoped dependencies
  • ViewModel layer:
  • consume use cases/repositories via constructor injection

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. App starts and creates root component.
  2. Android component creates child scope.
  3. ViewModel receives injected dependencies.
  4. Runtime resolves graph lazily/eagerly based on usage.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Critical component lifetimes:

  • SingletonComponent for process-wide services
  • ActivityRetainedComponent for config-safe objects
  • ViewModelComponent for screen logic scope
  • ActivityComponent/FragmentComponent for UI-bound dependencies

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@HiltViewModel
class SettingsViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val loadSettings: LoadSettingsUseCase
) : ViewModel()

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetworkModule {
    @Provides
    @Singleton
    fun provideApi(client: OkHttpClient): AppApi = AppApi(client)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Hilt vs raw Dagger: what changes practically?
  • Which scope should this dependency use?
  • When do you need an entry point?
  • How do you test Hilt-heavy modules?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• keep modules close to feature ownership boundaries
  • avoid blanket singleton usage for mutable objects
  • monitor annotation-processing cost in large projects
  • document scope conventions for onboarding

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • standardized DI architecture and fast team adoption
  • fewer custom graph plumbing errors
  • Cons:
  • reduced flexibility for exotic graph patterns
  • generated code errors can be hard for new devs

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior engineers should explain scope discipline and governance. Most Hilt failures at scale are ownership and lifecycle design issues, not missing annotations.

docs.title: Modularization strategies
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Modularization improves build performance and ownership clarity when boundaries reflect business capabilities and dependency direction rules.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• split by feature ownership and change cadence
  • keep API surface explicit and minimal
  • avoid cyclic dependencies between modules
  • enforce contracts through architecture checks

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• App shell module:
  • startup wiring, global navigation graph, DI root
  • Core/platform modules:
  • shared infrastructure (network, logging, analytics)
  • Feature modules:
  • feature UI orchestration and local domain policies
  • Shared contract modules:
  • interfaces/events used across features

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Feature UI triggers action in feature ViewModel.
  2. ViewModel calls feature/domain use case.
  3. Use case uses contracts from shared/core modules.
  4. Data module implementation executes and returns domain results.
  5. Feature maps domain output to UI state.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Common module patterns:

  • vertical feature slices (:feature:checkout, :feature:profile)
  • horizontal platform modules (:core:network, :core:database)
  • contract-only modules for inter-feature communication

Tooling to keep boundaries healthy:

  • dependency graph visualization
  • forbidden dependency lint rules
  • API/ABI boundary checks in CI

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// In :feature:orders-api
interface OrdersNavigator {
    fun openOrderDetails(orderId: String)
}

// In :feature:orders-impl
class OrdersNavigatorImpl(
    private val navController: NavController
) : OrdersNavigator {
    override fun openOrderDetails(orderId: String) {
        navController.navigate("orders/$orderId")
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When does modularization become over-engineering?
  • How do you handle shared code without creating a "god core" module?
  • API vs implementation dependency - what changes in build behavior?
  • How do teams migrate a monolith incrementally?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• start with a few high-value boundaries, then iterate
  • assign explicit owners per module
  • define deprecation/migration policy for shared APIs
  • measure build and integration metrics continuously

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • parallel team delivery and safer refactoring
  • improved incremental build performance
  • Cons:
  • coordination overhead for shared contracts
  • potential over-fragmentation and dependency friction

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior engineers should connect module boundaries to team topology. Good architecture reduces cross-team blocking and makes ownership visible.

docs.title: Mvi and udf
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: MVI and UDF emphasize explicit state transitions and predictable data flow. They are especially useful for complex screens where event ordering and side effects must stay debuggable.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• immutable UI state as render input
  • intent/action as user or system event
  • reducer as pure state-transition function
  • effect channel for one-time side effects

UDF is the principle; MVI is a concrete implementation style.

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• UI layer:
  • renders UiState
  • emits intents/actions
  • ViewModel/store:
  • reduces intents into new state
  • coordinates side effects through use cases
  • Domain/data layers:
  • execute business and integration work
  • map results/errors to reducer inputs

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. User action emits an intent.
  2. Intent enters reducer/store pipeline.
  3. Reducer computes new UiState.
  4. UI re-renders from state.
  5. One-time effects are emitted separately (navigation/snackbar/logging).

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
A practical Android setup often keeps a single state store per screen.

Key internal design choices:

  • single reducer vs split reducers by feature section
  • serialized intent processing for determinism
  • explicit effect middleware/interactor boundaries
  • state persistence strategy for process recreation

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
data class ProfileUiState(
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val user: UserUi? = null,
    val error: String? = null
)

sealed interface ProfileIntent {
    data object Load : ProfileIntent
    data object Retry : ProfileIntent
}

private fun reduce(state: ProfileUiState, intent: ProfileIntent): ProfileUiState {
    return when (intent) {
        ProfileIntent.Load,
        ProfileIntent.Retry -> state.copy(isLoading = true, error = null)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• MVI vs MVVM: when is MVI worth the overhead?
  • How do you model one-time events without replay bugs?
  • Should reducers be pure functions?
  • How do you prevent state explosion on large screens?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• keep intent vocabulary small and domain-oriented
  • avoid giant monolithic reducers by composing feature state slices
  • enforce state/effect separation in code reviews
  • log intent -> state transitions for incident debugging

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • deterministic behavior and easier debugging
  • better reasoning about concurrency/order
  • Cons:
  • extra ceremony and boilerplate
  • larger state models can become hard to maintain

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior candidates should discuss where MVI is selectively applied. Strong teams often combine MVVM structure with UDF discipline, rather than forcing strict MVI everywhere.

docs.title: Mvvm and viewmodel
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: MVVM remains the most common Android app architecture baseline. Its strength is separating rendering concerns from orchestration and data access.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• UI renders state, not repositories directly
  • ViewModel owns screen state and user intent handling
  • repositories/use cases provide business data
  • lifecycle-aware state exposure prevents UI loss on rotation

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• View (Activity/Fragment/Compose screen):
  • collect state
  • dispatch user actions
  • ViewModel:
  • transform domain outputs into UI models
  • coordinate async work and retries
  • Data/domain layer:
  • implement business and source policies

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. View dispatches action (onRetry, onRefresh, input change).
  2. ViewModel updates loading/intermediate state.
  3. ViewModel invokes use case or repository.
  4. Result maps to new immutable UiState.
  5. View observes and re-renders.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Production MVVM often uses:

  • StateFlow<UiState> for persistent state
  • separate event stream for one-time effects
  • reducer-style update helpers to keep transitions explicit
  • SavedStateHandle for small restorable fields

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
data class AccountUiState(
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val account: AccountUi? = null,
    val error: String? = null
)

class AccountViewModel(
    private val loadAccount: LoadAccountUseCase,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle
) : ViewModel() {
    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(AccountUiState())
    val uiState: StateFlow<AccountUiState> = _uiState
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Where does business logic end and UI logic begin?
  • Should ViewModel call repository directly or via use cases?
  • How do you model transient events in MVVM?
  • What usually makes a ViewModel "too fat"?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• keep ViewModel APIs small and explicit
  • avoid Android framework objects in domain contracts
  • standardize result/error mapping to reduce inconsistency
  • audit long-running jobs for lifecycle leaks

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • low ceremony and strong team familiarity
  • easy incremental adoption
  • Cons:
  • ViewModel bloat risk without architecture guardrails
  • inconsistent event/state modeling across teams

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level answers should describe how MVVM evolved in real codebases: what was pushed into use cases, what remained in ViewModel, and how teams enforced consistency at scale.

docs.title: Navigation and deep link architecture
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Navigation and Deep Link Architecture Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Navigation architecture should be contract-driven, testable, and module-aware. Deep links should be treated as external APIs that require compatibility and security considerations.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• destination contracts over raw string usage
  • route argument validation at boundaries
  • deep links as versioned external entry points
  • ownership of back stack behavior per app shell/feature shell

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation/navigation layer:
  • route to destinations and map arguments
  • execute UI-level transitions
  • Feature layer:
  • expose destination entry contracts
  • keep internal navigation details encapsulated
  • Platform/security layer:
  • validate deep link origins and payloads
  • enforce auth and feature-gating requirements

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Navigation event occurs (user action or deep link intent).
  2. Router validates destination and arguments.
  3. Feature entry point receives contract-safe input.
  4. Feature ViewModel loads state based on IDs/keys.
  5. UI renders and handles back behavior with explicit policy.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Recommended patterns:

  • central route registry with typed helpers
  • feature-level navigation interfaces
  • deep-link parser + validator pipeline
  • fallback path for unsupported or stale links

Avoid passing heavyweight mutable objects through routes; pass stable IDs and rehydrate from repository/domain layers.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
sealed interface AppRoute {
    data object Home : AppRoute
    data class OrderDetails(val orderId: String) : AppRoute
}

fun NavController.navigate(route: AppRoute) {
    when (route) {
        AppRoute.Home -> navigate("home")
        is AppRoute.OrderDetails -> navigate("orders/${route.orderId}")
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How do you design navigation for multi-module apps?
  • Where should deep link validation and auth checks happen?
  • How do you keep route contracts backward compatible?
  • What are common back-stack bugs and how do you prevent them?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• log deep-link parse failures and destination fallbacks
  • keep route schema changes backwards-compatible where possible
  • test cold-start deep links, authenticated flows, and process-death recovery
  • document cross-feature navigation contracts as stable APIs

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • clearer ownership and safer feature independence
  • better QA and observability for routing issues
  • Cons:
  • typed contract layers add upfront complexity
  • migration cost from ad-hoc navigation can be high

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong senior answers link navigation architecture to product reliability. At scale, deep links are integration points with marketing, web, and partner systems, so architecture must prioritize compatibility, security, and diagnostics.

docs.title: Offline first and sync
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Offline-first architecture treats local data as primary for reads and resilience. Network becomes synchronization infrastructure, not a mandatory read dependency.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• local-first reads for responsiveness and availability
  • queued writes with retry/backoff
  • explicit sync lifecycle and observability
  • deterministic conflict resolution policy

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation:
  • render local-backed state immediately
  • show sync status/errors transparently
  • Domain/use cases:
  • apply business invariants before enqueueing writes
  • Data/sync engine:
  • persist write queue
  • schedule pull/push sync
  • reconcile conflicts and update canonical store

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. User action writes to local store (or queue + local mutation).
  2. UI reflects updated local state optimistically.
  3. Sync worker pushes pending operations.
  4. Server response is reconciled and persisted.
  5. Canonical local state emits final representation.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Typical internal components:

  • local DB as SSOT
  • operation queue with metadata (attempt count, timestamps)
  • sync orchestrator (WorkManager + backoff)
  • merge/conflict policy module

Conflict handling examples:

  • last-write-wins for low-risk fields
  • version-based merge for collaborative entities
  • user-assisted merge for critical records

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
data class PendingOp(
    val id: String,
    val entityId: String,
    val type: String,
    val payload: String,
    val attempt: Int
)

interface SyncCoordinator {
    suspend fun enqueueWrite(op: PendingOp)
    suspend fun runSyncCycle()
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How do you guarantee eventual consistency?
  • When is optimistic UI unsafe?
  • How do you avoid infinite retry loops?
  • Where should conflict resolution policy live?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• instrument queue depth, sync latency, and conflict rate
  • use idempotency keys for retried write operations
  • provide backpressure when backend/system health degrades
  • ensure secure local storage for sensitive offline data

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • resilient UX under poor connectivity
  • smoother user interaction latency
  • Cons:
  • higher complexity in sync and reconciliation logic
  • larger operational/debugging surface area

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Staff-level answers connect architecture with operations: what metrics triggered incidents, how policies evolved, and how teams balanced consistency guarantees vs product latency goals.

docs.title: Production tradeoffs and decision making
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Production Tradeoffs and Decision-Making Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Architecture decisions are context-bound tradeoffs, not universal truths. Senior interviews often evaluate decision quality under constraints, not pattern memorization.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• explicit decision framing (problem, options, constraints)
  • ADRs to document rationale and consequences
  • risk-driven architecture (failure modes first)
  • feedback loops through operational metrics

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Feature teams:
  • propose and validate local architecture decisions
  • Platform/architecture leads:
  • define cross-system guardrails
  • Engineering leadership:
  • align technical decisions with product and org constraints

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Problem statement and constraints are captured.
  2. Candidate options are evaluated against quality attributes.
  3. Decision is recorded with expected outcomes and risks.
  4. Implementation ships with observability hooks.
  5. Metrics/postmortems refine future decisions.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Useful decision tools:

  • quality attribute matrix (latency, reliability, maintainability, cost)
  • blast-radius analysis for boundary changes
  • migration plans with rollback strategy
  • decision expiry review for long-lived assumptions

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// ADR metadata model example.
data class ArchitectureDecision(
    val id: String,
    val context: String,
    val decision: String,
    val consequences: List<String>
)

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How do you choose between speed and maintainability?
  • What does a strong architecture proposal include?
  • How do you know when to revisit old decisions?
  • How do you communicate tradeoffs to non-architect stakeholders?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• require written rationale for high-impact architecture changes
  • define measurable success/failure criteria before rollout
  • include rollback plans in design reviews
  • revisit major decisions after incidents or scale shifts

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • better decision traceability and institutional learning
  • reduced repeated debate on solved problems
  • Cons:
  • additional process overhead
  • risk of documentation drift without ownership

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong senior/staff answers show structured reasoning. They explain what was chosen, what was rejected, what risks were accepted, and how outcomes were measured.

docs.title: Reactive architecture with flows
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Reactive Architecture with Flows Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Reactive architecture models data and UI as streams over time. In Android, StateFlow and Flow pipelines enable lifecycle-aware rendering and clearer state propagation across layers.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• persistent UI state stream (StateFlow)
  • one-off event stream (SharedFlow/Channel)
  • upstream operators for mapping/filtering/debouncing
  • structured concurrency and cancellation-aware collection

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation:
  • collect state streams and render
  • collect event streams for transient effects
  • ViewModel/domain:
  • merge intents and data streams
  • expose immutable state and explicit events
  • Data:
  • expose source streams (DB/network sync updates)

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Source streams emit changes (DB/network/user intent).
  2. ViewModel combines/transforms streams.
  3. New UiState emits via StateFlow.
  4. UI collects with lifecycle awareness.
  5. Transient actions emit via dedicated event stream.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Design choices that matter:

  • where to combine streams (domain vs ViewModel)
  • replay/buffer configuration for event channels
  • backpressure and sampling strategy on high-frequency streams
  • cancellation boundaries tied to lifecycle scope

Pitfall to avoid: representing one-time navigation/snackbar as persistent state flags.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
class SearchViewModel(
    observeQuery: Flow<String>,
    private val repository: SearchRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    val uiState: StateFlow<SearchUiState> = observeQuery
        .debounce(300)
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .flatMapLatest { query -> repository.search(query) }
        .map { results -> SearchUiState(results = results) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchUiState())
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• StateFlow vs SharedFlow for UI architecture?
  • Where should operators live: UI, ViewModel, or domain?
  • How do you prevent duplicate collectors and wasted work?
  • How do you model retries in stream pipelines?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• set explicit sharing policies (WhileSubscribed, timeout)
  • instrument stream latency and emission volume
  • centralize error mapping for consistent UX behavior
  • guard expensive upstream work with memoization/cache strategies

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • composable data pipelines and clear async modeling
  • strong lifecycle/cancellation semantics
  • Cons:
  • operator chains can become hard to reason about
  • debugging complex stream interactions requires discipline

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior engineers should discuss stream contract governance: what constitutes state vs event, where transformations belong, and how to keep reactive pipelines understandable across teams.

docs.title: Repository pattern and data sources
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Repository Pattern and Data Sources Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Repository architecture abstracts data origin and centralizes consistency policy. In production Android apps, repositories are where cache, sync, and fallback logic should live instead of leaking into ViewModels.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• repository exposes stable domain-facing API
  • local and remote sources remain implementation details
  • single source of truth (SSOT) enforced at repository boundary
  • mapping and error normalization happen before upstream exposure

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation/ViewModel:
  • consume repository through use cases/contracts
  • avoid source-specific logic
  • Domain:
  • define repository interfaces and business semantics
  • Data:
  • implement source orchestration
  • handle persistence/network/retry policy

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Consumer requests data from repository.
  2. Repository reads canonical local source.
  3. Freshness rules decide whether remote fetch is needed.
  4. Remote result is validated/mapped and persisted.
  5. Updated canonical source emits new data upstream.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Typical repository internals:

  • remote source adapter (API)
  • local source adapter (DB/cache)
  • mapper layer (DTO <-> entity <-> UI model)
  • policy engine (TTL, backoff, conflict handling)

Important anti-patterns:

  • leaking Retrofit/Room types to domain/UI
  • duplicating fetch policy across features
  • bypassing repository for "quick fixes"

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
interface ArticleRepository {
    fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>>
    suspend fun refreshArticles(force: Boolean = false)
}

class ArticleRepositoryImpl(
    private val api: ArticleApi,
    private val dao: ArticleDao,
    private val clock: Clock
) : ArticleRepository {
    override fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>> = dao.observeAll()

    override suspend fun refreshArticles(force: Boolean) {
        if (force || dao.isStale(clock.now())) {
            val remote = api.getArticles()
            dao.replaceAll(remote.map { it.toEntity() })
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Should repositories return Flow, suspend, or both?
  • Where should mapping happen?
  • How do you enforce SSOT in multi-feature apps?
  • Repository vs use case: where do rules belong?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• document freshness and retry policies explicitly
  • include tracing around source decisions (local vs remote)
  • protect write paths with idempotency/retry semantics
  • keep repository APIs stable to minimize cross-team churn

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • consistency and reuse of data policy
  • lower UI-layer complexity
  • Cons:
  • repository can become a god object without boundaries
  • policy complexity grows with product scope

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level answers should discuss repository ownership and governance. At scale, success depends on keeping repository contracts stable while letting data-source implementations evolve safely.

docs.title: Scalability and team topologies
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Scalability and Team Topologies Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Application architecture and team architecture co-evolve. Technical boundaries that ignore ownership and communication patterns usually fail at scale.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Conway's Law impact on module boundaries
  • explicit ownership for code and contracts
  • integration points as socio-technical bottlenecks
  • platform enablement for shared standards

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Feature teams:
  • own feature modules, quality, and runtime outcomes
  • Platform/core teams:
  • provide shared infrastructure and guardrails
  • Architecture governance:
  • define and evolve boundary standards

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Team-owned feature emits requirements for shared capabilities.
  2. Platform modules expose stable contracts.
  3. Feature integrations consume contracts and report regressions.
  4. Governance loop adjusts contracts/tools based on delivery friction.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Patterns that help team scale:

  • clear module ownership metadata
  • ADR process for high-impact decisions
  • automated dependency policy checks
  • release and rollback strategy per boundary

Anti-patterns:

  • shared "misc" modules without ownership
  • cross-feature internals access as shortcuts
  • architecture decisions undocumented after implementation

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Example ownership metadata representation.
data class ModuleOwner(
    val module: String,
    val team: String,
    val slackChannel: String
)

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How does architecture reduce cross-team blocking?
  • What boundaries should a platform team own?
  • How do you measure architecture scalability?
  • How do you evolve ownership during re-orgs?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• publish ownership and dependency maps
  • enforce compatibility/deprecation windows for shared APIs
  • include architecture health KPIs in engineering reviews
  • align incident response with module ownership

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • predictable delivery and clearer accountability
  • faster onboarding through explicit boundaries
  • Cons:
  • governance overhead
  • coordination cost for cross-cutting changes

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Staff candidates should discuss tradeoffs between autonomy and standardization. The best systems provide local team freedom with global guardrails.

docs.title: Service locator and anti patterns
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Service Locator and Anti-Patterns Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Service Locator can bootstrap dependency access quickly, but it often hides coupling and weakens architectural clarity.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• global or scoped registry returns dependencies at runtime
  • call sites hide concrete dependency requirements
  • implicit wiring increases runtime failure risk
  • testing often needs registry mutation/reset behavior

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Locator layer:
  • stores and returns object instances/providers
  • Consumers:
  • pull dependencies rather than receive them explicitly
  • Test layer:
  • overrides/replaces registry entries for test isolation

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Consumer requests service from locator.
  2. Locator resolves key/provider.
  3. Dependency is returned and used.
  4. Missing/incorrect registration fails at runtime.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Why this degrades over time:

  • hidden dependency graph at call sites
  • hard-to-track lifecycle ownership
  • mutation-heavy test setup
  • implicit global state leakage

Controlled usage can be acceptable in tiny apps or transitional migration phases.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
object ServiceLocator {
    lateinit var analytics: Analytics
}

class HomeViewModel : ViewModel() {
    fun trackOpen() {
        ServiceLocator.analytics.log("home_open")
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is constructor DI generally preferred?
  • Is Service Locator always an anti-pattern?
  • How do hidden dependencies hurt testability?
  • How would you migrate incrementally to DI?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid introducing new locator-based dependencies
  • migrate hotspots first (core services, ViewModels)
  • keep temporary adapters during transition
  • add static checks to block direct global locator usage

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • fast startup for simple prototypes
  • low initial ceremony
  • Cons:
  • hidden coupling and brittle tests
  • runtime misconfiguration failures
  • poor fit for multi-team codebases

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior candidates should present migration strategy, not just anti-pattern labeling. Good answers discuss risk-managed refactors and compatibility bridges while moving toward explicit DI.

docs.title: State management and ssot
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: State Management and SSOT Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: State management is an ownership problem first, and a UI rendering problem second. Single Source of Truth (SSOT) prevents divergence between competing state copies.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• one canonical state owner per concern
  • immutable UI state models for deterministic rendering
  • explicit event pathways for mutations
  • derived/read-only projections for consumers

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation:
  • render UiState
  • emit intents/events only
  • Domain/ViewModel:
  • process intents into state transitions
  • orchestrate use-case calls
  • Data/repository:
  • maintain canonical persisted state
  • apply sync/cache policies

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. User emits event (refresh/filter/retry).
  2. ViewModel processes and invokes use case.
  3. Use case/repository updates authoritative state.
  4. State stream emits new model.
  5. UI re-renders from latest immutable state.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
SSOT is usually implemented with local persistence as canonical read path, then upstream refresh updates that store.

Key internal patterns:

  • state reducers for predictable transitions
  • state vs event channel separation
  • idempotent write handling where possible

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
data class FeedUiState(
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val items: List<FeedItem> = emptyList(),
    val errorMessage: String? = null
)

class FeedViewModel(
    private val observeFeed: ObserveFeedUseCase,
    private val refreshFeed: RefreshFeedUseCase
) : ViewModel() {
    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(FeedUiState())
    val uiState: StateFlow<FeedUiState> = _uiState
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why separate one-time events from persistent state?
  • Where should SSOT live: ViewModel or repository?
  • How do you prevent stale state races?
  • Is immutable state always required?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid hidden mutable singletons as state owners
  • define clear state transition rules per feature
  • include correlation IDs/log context for state-related failures
  • test high-frequency event paths and cancellation behavior

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • easier debugging and replay reasoning
  • lower inconsistency risk across features
  • Cons:
  • more explicit modeling and boilerplate
  • strict patterns can feel heavy for trivial screens

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level discussions should include failure modes: state divergence, duplicate write paths, and event replay bugs. Mature teams treat state contracts as product-critical APIs.

docs.title: Testing architecture and testability
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Testing Architecture and Testability Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Testability is an architectural property. Systems with explicit dependencies, clear boundaries, and deterministic state transitions are easier to verify and evolve.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• dependency injection for replaceable collaborators
  • contract-driven boundaries between modules/layers
  • deterministic state reducers and use-case behavior
  • test pyramid with fast lower-level coverage

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Unit tests:
  • verify use cases, reducers, mappers
  • Integration tests:
  • verify repository/source orchestration
  • UI tests:
  • verify critical user journeys and rendering contracts

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Provide fake or test-double dependencies.
  2. Trigger intent/use-case action.
  3. Observe state/output transitions.
  4. Assert deterministic expected behavior.
  5. Validate boundary contracts in integration scenarios.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Key architecture decisions for testability:

  • constructor injection everywhere possible
  • pure mapping/reducer functions
  • abstraction boundaries at network/db/platform edges
  • explicit time/thread control in async pipelines

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
class LoginViewModelTest {
    private val repository = FakeAuthRepository()
    private val viewModel = LoginViewModel(LoginUseCase(repository))

    @Test
    fun emitsErrorStateWhenCredentialsInvalid() = runTest {
        viewModel.onSubmit("bad", "creds")
        assertTrue(viewModel.uiState.value is LoginUiState.Error)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What should be unit vs integration tested?
  • How do you test one-time events?
  • How do you keep UI tests stable and valuable?
  • How do contract tests help modular teams?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• prioritize deterministic fast tests in CI gates
  • track flaky-test rate as architecture health metric
  • use fixture/data builders to reduce test duplication
  • enforce test ownership at module boundaries

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • safer refactors and faster incident recovery
  • clearer confidence signals for releases
  • Cons:
  • upfront effort for harnesses/fakes
  • maintenance cost for poor test design

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level answers should include test strategy evolution. The goal is not 100% coverage, but high signal coverage aligned with risky paths and architectural boundaries.

docs.title: Ui state and event modeling
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: UI State and Event Modeling Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: UI architecture quality depends on modeling state and events explicitly. Clear contracts prevent sticky-event bugs, duplicated retries, and inconsistent error rendering.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• persistent UiState for renderable screen model
  • transient event channel for one-time actions
  • error taxonomy mapped to user-actionable outcomes
  • retry policy as explicit state transition, not ad-hoc callbacks

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• UI:
  • render UiState
  • react to event stream once
  • ViewModel/store:
  • own state transitions and event emission
  • map technical errors to UX-safe states
  • Domain/data:
  • provide normalized result/error models

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Action intent enters ViewModel.
  2. Use case/repository returns success or categorized failure.
  3. ViewModel emits new UiState branch (loading/content/error/empty).
  4. Optional one-time event emits for toast/navigation/dialog.
  5. User retry intent triggers controlled transition.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Good model patterns:

  • sealed state branches for mutually exclusive UI modes
  • separate retry metadata (attempt count, next allowed time)
  • standardized error mapping layer (network/auth/business)
  • idempotent reducer updates for repeated events

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
sealed interface CheckoutUiState {
    data object Loading : CheckoutUiState
    data class Content(val total: String) : CheckoutUiState
    data class Error(val message: String, val canRetry: Boolean) : CheckoutUiState
}

sealed interface CheckoutEvent {
    data object ShowPaymentFailedToast : CheckoutEvent
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why not keep one-off events inside state?
  • How do you avoid event replay on rotation?
  • Where should retry backoff decisions live?
  • How do you keep error handling consistent across features?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• define shared UX error standards across teams
  • log error category and user action path for observability
  • cap auto-retry behavior to avoid backend abuse
  • add regression tests for event replay edge cases

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • clearer rendering logic and fewer race-condition bugs
  • easier incident analysis from explicit transitions
  • Cons:
  • more model classes and conventions to maintain
  • potential verbosity in simple screens

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior engineers should tie state modeling to product reliability. The best systems make failure states first-class, not bolt-ons added after incidents.

docs.title: Use cases and domain layer
docs.text: ← Back to Architecture

docs.title: Use Cases and Domain Layer Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Use cases encapsulate business actions so policy decisions are not scattered across ViewModels or repository implementations. A domain layer pays off when business behavior is complex or reused across features.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• use case = coherent business action
  • domain entities/value objects express business language
  • domain contracts isolate policy from framework details
  • composition of use cases supports larger workflows

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Presentation:
  • trigger use cases based on UI intent
  • render resulting state
  • Domain:
  • hold business rules and orchestration policies
  • remain framework-agnostic
  • Data:
  • fulfill domain contracts with integration details

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. UI emits intent.
  2. ViewModel invokes a use case.
  3. Use case applies domain rules and calls repository contracts.
  4. Repository/data layer executes integration work.
  5. Domain result is mapped to UI state.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Use-case design heuristics:

  • one clear business outcome per use case
  • avoid thin pass-through wrappers unless establishing boundary
  • compose related use cases for larger scenarios
  • keep input/output models domain-centric and stable

Common smell: "god use case" that mixes orchestration, validation, and technical error handling without separation.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
class PlaceOrderUseCase(
    private val cartRepository: CartRepository,
    private val paymentRepository: PaymentRepository,
    private val orderRepository: OrderRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(input: PlaceOrderInput): PlaceOrderResult {
        val cart = cartRepository.getActiveCart(input.userId)
        require(cart.items.isNotEmpty()) { "Cart cannot be empty" }

        val payment = paymentRepository.authorize(input.paymentMethod, cart.total)
        return orderRepository.createOrder(cart, payment)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When does a domain layer become over-engineering?
  • How many use cases per feature is too many?
  • Where should validation rules live?
  • How do you test use-case orchestration effectively?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• keep domain API naming aligned with product language
  • treat use-case signatures as long-lived contracts
  • add focused unit tests for business invariants
  • prevent Android framework leakage into domain types

docs.title: Scalability Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • better policy reuse and clearer business boundaries
  • improved testability and refactor safety
  • Cons:
  • additional indirection for simple CRUD apps
  • maintenance overhead if boundaries are poorly defined

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior candidates should explain how domain boundaries evolved with product complexity. Great answers include examples where introducing or removing a domain layer improved delivery and reliability outcomes.

docs.title: Animation in compose
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Compose animation APIs range from simple value transitions to coordinated multi-state motion systems.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• animate*AsState for simple property animation
  • AnimatedVisibility / AnimatedContent for content transitions
  • Transition APIs for coordinated animations

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Animation state updates over frames, driving recomposition and draw invalidation for animated properties.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• target state changes
  • animation engine interpolates values per frame
  • consumers recompose/draw with new frame values

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Model animation trigger state explicitly and avoid coupling animation state tightly with business domain state.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val alpha by animateFloatAsState(targetValue = if (expanded) 1f else 0f, label = "alpha")
Text("Details", modifier = Modifier.alpha(alpha))

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Which API to choose for simple vs complex transitions?
  • How do you reduce jank in animation-heavy screens?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• cap concurrent animations in dense lists
  • align motion spec with design system
  • test reduced-motion and accessibility cases

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Animation smoothness depends on stable frame budget; expensive recomposition or layout work during animation is a common jank source.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior candidates discuss animation as system design: API choice, consistency, performance budgeting, and UX intent.

docs.title: Compose basics and composable contract
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Compose Basics and Composable Contract Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Jetpack Compose shifts Android UI from imperative view mutation to declarative rendering. At interview level, the key message is: UI is a function of current state.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Declarative UI: describe desired UI, not mutation steps.
  • @Composable contract: function can emit UI into composition tree.
  • Composition tree: hierarchical structure produced by composables.
  • Identity by call position + keys: important for state retention.

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text:
Compose compiler rewrites composables into functions that receive a Composer and change-tracking flags. This enables restart groups, skipping, and remember slots.

Important internals to mention:

  • positional memoization model
  • compiler-generated group boundaries
  • runtime-managed tree diff/apply behavior

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
1. Initial composition executes composables and builds groups.
  2. Runtime tracks state reads for each group.
  3. On state change, affected groups are invalidated.
  4. Recomposition re-executes invalidated groups only.
  5. Apply phase updates UI nodes.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text:
For basics, state should follow this separation:

  • local ephemeral UI state with remember
  • restorable UI state with rememberSaveable
  • screen/business state in ViewModel

Avoid mixing state ownership across multiple layers without clear boundaries.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Composable
fun ProfileHeader(name: String, isOnline: Boolean) {
    Row {
        Text(text = name)
        if (isOnline) {
            Text(text = " • Online")
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun Counter() {
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
    Column {
        Text("Count: $count")
        Button(onClick = { count++ }) {
            Text("Increment")
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is Compose called declarative?
  • Is a composable lifecycle same as Activity lifecycle?
  • Why should composables avoid side effects during rendering?
  • How does Compose know which UI to update?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Keep composables small and single-purpose.
  • Pass explicit state + callbacks to improve testability.
  • Avoid hidden dependencies for business logic.
  • Use previews for fast UI iteration, but validate with tests.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
• Smaller, focused composables create cleaner recomposition boundaries.
  • Stable inputs improve skipping opportunities.
  • Excessive lambda/object allocation in hot paths can increase frame cost.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Strong senior answers connect API ergonomics to runtime behavior:

  • compiler inserts change tracking and restart groups
  • runtime re-executes selectively rather than re-rendering whole screen
  • architectural state boundaries directly influence performance characteristics

docs.title: Composer applier and runtime phases
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Composer, Applier, and Runtime Phases Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Composer computes structural updates, while Applier executes those updates on the target UI tree.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• composition phase (compute changes)
  • layout phase (measure/place)
  • draw phase (render)
  • applier operations (insert/move/remove/update)

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Compiler-generated composable code emits operations through Composer. Applier-specific implementations map operations to concrete UI nodes.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• invalidated groups are recomposed
  • composer records mutations
  • applier commits node operations
  • layout/draw run as required by invalidations

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: State changes can trigger different phase costs depending on whether they affect structure, layout constraints, or only drawing properties.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Composable
fun AlphaChip(text: String, enabled: Boolean) {
    Text(
        text = text,
        modifier = Modifier.alpha(if (enabled) 1f else 0.5f)
    )
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Is recomposition equivalent to layout + draw every time?
  • What responsibilities belong to composer vs applier?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• optimize based on phase bottleneck, not assumptions
  • profile structure/layout/draw costs separately

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: A change limited to draw properties is usually cheaper than one causing full layout recalculation.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior engineers explain phase-specific invalidation and use that model to pick targeted optimizations.

docs.title: Compositionlocal and context propagation
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: CompositionLocal and Context Propagation Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: CompositionLocal provides implicit dependency propagation through the compose tree. It is powerful for environment-like values and risky for hidden business dependencies.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• providers set values for subtree
  • consumers read local values without explicit params
  • great for theme/system ambient data

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Reads of locals are tracked like other composition inputs. Provider changes invalidate consumers in affected subtree.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• local provided at parent
  • descendants read local
  • provider value changes
  • dependent descendants recompose

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Use locals for cross-cutting environment values, not for feature business state ownership.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val LocalSpacing = compositionLocalOf { 8.dp }

@Composable
fun AppTheme(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalSpacing provides 12.dp) {
        content()
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When should you avoid CompositionLocal?
  • How does it differ from dependency injection?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• document every custom local clearly
  • keep number of custom locals manageable
  • provide test replacements for deterministic UI tests

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Broad provider updates can invalidate large subtrees; scope providers as tightly as practical.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level guidance: use CompositionLocal as environment plumbing, not as an escape hatch for architectural shortcuts.

docs.title: Derived state and remember updated state
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Derived State and rememberUpdatedState Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: These APIs solve two different problems: efficient derived calculations and safe access to latest values inside long-lived effects.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• derivedStateOf: memoize computed state by dependencies
  • rememberUpdatedState: update captured reference without restarting effect

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: derivedStateOf participates in snapshot observation. Recalculation happens only when dependencies change; downstream readers observe the derived state.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• source state changes
  • derived value invalidates if dependency changed
  • consumers recompose with updated computed value

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Use derived state for expensive projections, not for trivial string concatenation. Use updated-state for callback freshness in timers/listeners.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Composable
fun TimedAction(onTimeout: () -> Unit) {
    val latestOnTimeout by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(3_000)
        latestOnTimeout()
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why not key LaunchedEffect with callback directly?
  • Does derivedStateOf always improve performance?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid premature optimization
  • verify with profiling when derived state adds value
  • document intent when using updated-state to avoid confusion

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: derivedStateOf can reduce unnecessary invalidations in hot UI paths such as scroll and search filtering.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong answers include tradeoffs: both APIs add complexity, so they should be used where correctness or measurable performance benefit exists.

docs.title: Effects coroutines and lifecycle
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Effects, Coroutines, and Lifecycle Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, and rememberCoroutineScope connect coroutines and callback-style resources to composition lifecycle.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• LaunchedEffect: composition-scoped coroutine
  • DisposableEffect: setup + guaranteed cleanup
  • rememberCoroutineScope: manual event-driven launches

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Effect jobs are attached to composition scope. Key changes trigger cancellation and restart for keyed effects.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• enter composition -> start keyed effect
  • key change -> cancel old job, launch new one
  • leave composition -> cancel/dispose deterministically

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Use rememberUpdatedState when effect must keep running but consume latest callback.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Composable
fun LocationObserver(onLocation: (Location) -> Unit) {
    DisposableEffect(Unit) {
        val listener = startLocationUpdates(onLocation)
        onDispose { listener.stop() }
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• LaunchedEffect(Unit) vs rememberCoroutineScope?
  • How do you avoid stale lambda capture?
  • When is cleanup guaranteed?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid unstable keys for long-lived jobs
  • keep cleanup paths explicit
  • use lifecycle-aware collection in screen composables

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Frequent effect restart in scroll-heavy or rapidly changing UIs can become an invisible source of overhead.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Best answers show precise cancellation semantics and justify effect API choices using lifecycle and correctness constraints.

docs.title: Flow integration with compose
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Flow Integration with Compose Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Compose commonly consumes StateFlow and other Flows from ViewModel layers. This section focuses on lifecycle-aware collection and snapshot bridging.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• collect flow to UI state
  • lifecycle-aware collection on Android screens
  • separate state streams from one-off event streams

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Flow emissions update Compose State, which invalidates dependent scopes and triggers recomposition scheduling.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• collector receives emission
  • state holder updates
  • dependent composables recompose
  • unchanged branches may still be skipped

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Prefer immutable UiState and explicit event channels for navigation/snackbar.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Composable
fun HomeRoute(viewModel: HomeViewModel) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    HomeScreen(state = state, onRetry = viewModel::retry)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• collectAsState vs collectAsStateWithLifecycle?
  • How to model one-time events safely?
  • Why use snapshotFlow?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid collecting high-frequency streams without need
  • debounce/filter upstream when possible
  • verify cancellation when screen leaves foreground

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Excess emissions with large UI models can amplify recomposition work. Consider state granularity and emission strategy.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior candidates should explain end-to-end data flow from repository emission to recomposition behavior and lifecycle management.

docs.title: Layout measure draw pipeline
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Layout, Measure, and Draw Pipeline Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Compose rendering uses measure, layout, and draw phases with clear responsibilities. Understanding phase cost is key for UI performance interviews.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• constraints flow downward
  • sizes flow upward
  • placement happens in layout block
  • draw happens after geometry is finalized

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: LayoutNode and measure policies coordinate child measurement and placement, then draw modifiers and content execute in draw phase.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• composition emits layout tree
  • measure computes bounds
  • layout places children
  • draw renders visuals

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Structure state so frequent changes only affect necessary phases where possible.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Composable
fun TwoPane(modifier: Modifier = Modifier, left: @Composable () -> Unit, right: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    Layout(content = { left(); right() }, modifier = modifier) { measurables, constraints ->
        val half = constraints.maxWidth / 2
        val leftPlaceable = measurables[0].measure(constraints.copy(maxWidth = half))
        val rightPlaceable = measurables[1].measure(constraints.copy(maxWidth = half))

        layout(constraints.maxWidth, maxOf(leftPlaceable.height, rightPlaceable.height)) {
            leftPlaceable.placeRelative(0, 0)
            rightPlaceable.placeRelative(half, 0)
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What is intrinsic measurement and when is it costly?
  • Why can nested unconstrained layouts cause performance issues?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid repeated expensive measurement logic
  • validate custom layouts on low-end devices

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Phase-aware optimizations outperform generic "optimize recomposition" advice.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level candidates reason about constraints and phase invalidations when debugging layout jank.

docs.title: Lazy layouts and list performance
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Lazy Layouts and List Performance Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: LazyColumn/LazyRow optimize large collections by composing only needed items, but identity and item-content design determine real performance.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• lazy item composition
  • stable keys for identity
  • item-level state ownership
  • list scroll and prefetch behavior

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Lazy layouts maintain item providers and viewport-driven composition windows. Wrong keys can break slot reuse and state placement.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• viewport changes trigger item composition/disposal
  • changed item state invalidates affected rows
  • stable keys preserve item identity through moves

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Keep per-item transient state inside keyed item scope; keep business state in ViewModel.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
LazyColumn {
    items(messages, key = { it.id }) { message ->
        MessageRow(message = message)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why do items "jump" without keys?
  • How do you reduce jank on long feeds?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid expensive work inside item lambdas
  • use paging/windowing for very large data sets
  • profile with realistic datasets and devices

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: List performance regressions often come from unstable models, heavy item composition, and missing keys rather than lazy container itself.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong answers combine architecture (state granularity) with runtime mechanics (identity, reuse, and viewport-driven composition).

docs.title: Modifier chain and node graph
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Modifier Chain and Node Graph Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Modifier order changes behavior because each modifier wraps/transforms node behavior for input, layout, drawing, and semantics.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• left-to-right chain semantics
  • layout vs draw vs input modifiers
  • semantics and accessibility modifiers

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Modifiers are represented in node structures and participate in phase-specific processing pipelines.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• modifier parameters change
  • relevant node chain updates
  • affected phases invalidate (layout/draw/input)

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Keep modifier state localized and avoid rebuilding long chains unnecessarily in hot paths.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
Modifier
    .padding(8.dp)
    .clip(RoundedCornerShape(8.dp))
    .clickable { onClick() }

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why does padding().clickable() differ from clickable().padding()?
  • Which modifiers impact semantics tree?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• standardize modifier ordering conventions in codebase
  • extract reusable modifier builders for consistency

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Long, frequently changing modifier chains can add overhead; prefer stable, reused chains where practical.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Good answers connect modifier order bugs to concrete runtime/UX outcomes (hit target, clipping, semantics, and jank).

docs.title: Navigation in compose
docs.text: ← Back to Compose

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Compose navigation should be treated as explicit route contracts, not ad-hoc string pushes. Maintainability comes from typed arguments and clear ownership of navigation decisions.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• route graph and destination contracts
  • argument passing by IDs
  • back stack semantics
  • deep link handling

docs.title: Runtime Internals
docs.text: Navigation state updates drive destination composable changes and back stack mutations. Each destination composes/disposes with navigation lifecycle transitions.

docs.title: Composition / Recomposition Flow
docs.text:
• event triggers navigation action
  • nav state mutates
  • destination composition changes
  • previous destination may remain on back stack

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Store screen state in destination-scoped ViewModels and avoid leaking navigation concerns into presentational child composables.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
