docs.title: Looper and handler
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Looper and Handler enable thread-safe message passing in Android. Looper processes messages in a queue, Handler sends messages to that queue and executes them on a specific thread. This is the foundation for multi-threading and the Binder system.

docs.title: What is Looper?
docs.text:
A Looper is a thread mechanism that: 1. Maintains a message queue 2. Continuously loops through it (hence "Looper") 3. Processes messages one at a time 4. Blocks when queue empty 

// Looper lifecycle
Looper.prepare()           // Create Looper for thread
// ...do work...
Looper.loop()              // Start infinite loop
// Code after loop() never reached until quit()

docs.title: Main Thread Looper
docs.text:
The main thread automatically has a Looper: 

// In ActivityThread (Android framework)
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    Looper.prepareMainLooper()
    // ... create activities ...
    Looper.loop()
}

docs.title: Background Thread Looper
docs.text:
Thread {
    Looper.prepare()       // Create Looper for this thread
    val handler = Handler()  // Handler uses this thread's Looper
    // Do work, Handler messages will be processed
    Looper.loop()          // Start processing messages
}.start()

docs.title:
// ❌ WRONG - second Looper.prepare() throws exception
Looper.prepare()
Looper.prepare()  // RuntimeException: already prepared
// ✅ CORRECT - 1 per thread max
Looper.prepare()
Looper.loop()  // Process messages on this thread
// After loop() returns, Looper.quit() was called
What is Handler?
docs.text:
Handler sends messages to a Looper's queue and executes callbacks on that Looper's thread. 

// Create handler attached to main thread Looper
val mainHandler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
// Create handler attached to current thread's Looper
val localHandler = Handler()
// Send work to execute on that thread
mainHandler.post {
    updateUI()  // Runs on main thread
}

docs.title: Handler Operations
docs.text:
post() - Execute Runnable immediately 

handler.post(Runnable { doWork() })
postDelayed() - Execute after delay 
handler.postDelayed(
    Runnable { doWork() },
    5000  // 5 seconds
)
postAtTime() - Execute at specific time 
handler.postAtTime(
    Runnable { doWork() },
    SystemClock.uptimeMillis() + 5000
)
sendMessage() - Send Message object 
val msg = Message.obtain().apply {
    what = MSG_UPDATE_UI
    arg1 = userId
}
handler.sendMessage(msg)
sendDelayedMessage() 
handler.sendMessageDelayed(msg, 5000)

docs.title: What is HandlerThread
docs.text:
HandlerThread is a Thread subclass that automatically creates and starts a Looper. 

// ❌ Manual Looper setup
val thread = Thread {
    Looper.prepare()
    val handler = Handler()
    // do work
    Looper.loop()
}
thread.start()
// ✅ Simpler with HandlerThread
val handlerThread = HandlerThread("MyThread")
handlerThread.start()
val handler = Handler(handlerThread.looper)

docs.title: HandlerThread Use Cases
docs.text:
Background Image Processing: 

val backgroundThread = HandlerThread("ImageProcessing")
backgroundThread.start()
val imageHandler = Handler(backgroundThread.looper)
imageHandler.post {
    val bitmap = processBitmap(largeImage)
    mainHandler.post { displayBitmap(bitmap) }
}
Database Operations: 
val dbThread = HandlerThread("DatabaseIO")
dbThread.start()
val dbHandler = Handler(dbThread.looper)
dbHandler.post {
    val user = database.userDao().loadUser(userId)
    mainHandler.post { displayUser(user) }
}

docs.title:
override fun onDestroy() {
    handlerThread.quit()  // Or quitSafely()
    super.onDestroy()
}
The Problem
docs.text:
Delayed Handler messages can leak Activity context: 

class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        // Post delayed message
        handler.postDelayed({
            updateUI()  // Implicit 'this' reference
        }, 60000)
    }
    override fun onDestroy() {
        // ❌ Activity destroyed but message still in queue
        // Message queued for 60 seconds holds Activity reference
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}
Leak chain: 
Handler.MessageQueue → Message → Callback (Runnable with 'this')
                                  ↓
                              MyActivity (cannot GC)
                                  ↓
                              Views, resources (leaked)

docs.title: Solution 1: Remove Messages in onDestroy()
docs.text:
override fun onDestroy() {
    handler.removeCallbacksAndMessages(null)  // Remove all pending
    super.onDestroy()
}

docs.title: Solution 2: WeakReference Handler
docs.text:
class MyWeakHandler(activity: MyActivity) : Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) {
    private val activityRef = WeakReference(activity)
    override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
        val activity = activityRef.get()
        if (activity != null) {
            // Use activity
        }
    }
}
// Usage
val handler = MyWeakHandler(this)

docs.title:
// Coroutines handle cleanup automatically
viewModelScope.launch {
    delay(60000)
    updateUI()  // Auto-cancels if Activity destroyed
}
Message Object
docs.text:
data class Message(
    val what: Int = 0,              // Message type
    val arg1: Int = 0,              // Additional data
    val arg2: Int = 0,              // Additional data
    val obj: Any? = null,           // Payload
    val replyTo: Messenger? = null  // Reply to address
)

docs.title: MessageQueue
docs.text:
What it is:
├─ Infinite queue of Messages
├─ Added via Handler.sendMessage()
├─ Processed by Looper one at a time
└─ Ordered by time/priority

docs.title:
Queue:
[Message 1 @ t=0]
[Message 2 @ t=50]
[Message 3 @ t=100]
Looper processes in order:
t=0: Message 1 executed
t=50: Message 2 executed
t=100: Message 3 executed
Cross-Thread Communication
docs.text:
// Thread 1 (Background)
Thread {
    Looper.prepare()
    val bgHandler = Handler()
    mainHandler.post {
        // Signal to main thread
        updateUI("Done")
    }
    Looper.loop()
}.start()

docs.title:
val workerThread = HandlerThread("Worker")
workerThread.start()
val workerHandler = Handler(workerThread.looper)
workerHandler.post {
    // This runs on worker thread
    val data = heavyComputation()
    // Post back to main
    mainHandler.post {
        displayResult(data)
    }
}
Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: Why use Handler instead of just Thread.join()? A: Handler enables message-driven architecture. join() blocks caller. Handler queues work for later. Q: Can you have multiple Handlers on one Looper? A: Yes! Multiple Handlers can post to same Looper's queue. Q: What happens if you call Looper.loop() twice? A: RuntimeException - already preparing. Q: Is Looper thread-safe? A: MessageQueue is thread-safe. Can post from any thread, executes on Looper's thread.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text: ✅ Looper = message queue processor on a thread ✅ Handler = sends messages to Looper's queue ✅ HandlerThread = Thread with automatic Looper ✅ Main thread has Looper automatically ✅ postDelayed() can leak if not removed ✅ Use removeCallbacksAndMessages() in onDestroy() ✅ Coroutines often better than manual Handler management

docs.title: Memory leaks
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A memory leak in Android occurs when an object is no longer needed but remains referenced, preventing garbage collection. The result is growing memory usage, eventual OutOfMemoryError, and app crashes. Android-specific leaks often involve holding Context or Activity references in long-lived objects.

docs.title: Garbage Collector & Reachability
docs.text:
How GC Works: 

1. Mark phase: Find all reachable objects from GC roots
2. Sweep phase: Delete unreachable objects
3. Compact phase: Reorder memory

Unreachable objects = collected
Still referenced objects = kept in memory (even if unused)

docs.title: GC Roots (What keeps objects alive)
docs.text:
├─ Running threads
├─ Stack variables (local scope)
├─ Static references
├─ JNI references
├─ Monitored objects
└─ System classes

docs.title: Memory Leak Definition
docs.text:
Object A no longer needed
But still referenced by Object B
Object B still referenced by active code
Result: A never garbage collected → LEAK

docs.title: Pattern 1: Static Reference to Activity
docs.text:
class MyAnalytics {
    companion object {
        var activity: Activity? = null  // ❌ LEAK
    }

    fun trackEvent() {
        activity?.let { act ->
            // Activity reference never released
        }
    }
}

// In MainActivity
override fun onCreate() {
    MyAnalytics.activity = this
    // Activity destroyed, but MyAnalytics.activity still holds reference
}

Leak Chain: 

MyAnalytics.activity → MainActivity (static ref)
                    → Views
                    → Resources
                    ❌ ALL LEAKED

Fix: 

companion object {
    var context: Context? = null  // Use app context instead
}

override fun onCreate() {
    MyAnalytics.context = applicationContext  // Won't leak
}

docs.title: Pattern 2: Inner Class Holding Outer Activity
docs.text:
class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    inner class MyThread : Thread() {  // ❌ LEAK
        override fun run() {
            Thread.sleep(60000)
            // During sleep, implicit 'this@MyActivity' ref held
        }
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        MyThread().start()  // Activity held for 60 seconds
    }
}

Leak Chain: 

MyThread → (implicit this$0) → MyActivity → All resources

Fix: 

private static class MyThread extends Thread {  // Static = no implicit Activity ref
    private final WeakReference<MyActivity> activityRef;

    MyThread(MyActivity activity) {
        this.activityRef = new WeakReference<>(activity);
    }

    override fun run() {
        val activity = activityRef.get()  // May be null if GC'd
        if (activity != null) {
            // Use activity
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Pattern 3: Handler with Delayed Messages
docs.text:
class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        handler.postDelayed({
            // Runnable implicitly holds 'this' Activity reference
            updateUI()  // This runs 60s later
        }, 60000)
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        // ❌ If not removed, Activity leaked for 60s
    }
}

Leak Chain: 

Handler.MessageQueue → Message → Callback (Runnable)
                                          → (implicit this) → Activity

Fix: 

override fun onDestroy() {
    handler.removeCallbacksAndMessages(null)  // Remove pending messages
    super.onDestroy()
}

// OR use coroutines (auto-cleanup)
viewModel.doWork()  // Auto-cancelled when Activity destroyed

docs.title: Pattern 4: Unregistered Listener/Broadcast Receiver
docs.text:
class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        eventBus.register(this)  // ❌ If never unregistered

        // Activity destroyed but still registered
        // EventBus holds reference → Activity can't be GC'd
    }

    // ❌ onDestroy never called, or unregister missing
}

Fix: 

override fun onDestroy() {
    eventBus.unregister(this)
    super.onDestroy()
}

docs.title: Pattern 5: Long-Lived Singleton Holding Activity Context
docs.text:
object MySingleton {
    var context: Context? = null  // Activity context stored
}

class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        MySingleton.context = this  // ❌ Activity stored in singleton
        // Activity destroyed but singleton still holds reference
    }
}

Fix: 

object MySingleton {
    var context: Context? = null
}

class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        MySingleton.context = applicationContext  // App context - safe
    }
}

docs.title: WeakReference
docs.text:
val weakRef = WeakReference<Activity>(activity)

// Usage
val activity = weakRef.get()
if (activity != null) {
    activity.doSomething()
}
// If no strong reference elsewhere, GC collects immediately

When to use: - Storing references to Activities - Objects that can be recreated - Short-term caching

docs.title: SoftReference
docs.text:
val softRef = SoftReference<Bitmap>(bitmap)

// Usage
val bitmap = softRef.get()
if (bitmap != null) {
    drawBitmap(bitmap)
}
// GC keeps alive unless memory pressure

When to use: - Image caches - Objects expensive to recreate - Long-term caching

docs.title: LeakCanary (BEST TOOL)
docs.text:
Setup: 

debugImplementation 'com.squareup.leakcanary:leakcanary-android:2.12'

Features: - Automatically detects Activity leaks - Shows leak chain in logcat - Provides fix suggestions - No code changes needed

How it works: 

1. Watches destroyed activities
2. Forces GC
3. Checks if still in memory
4. If yes: Dumps heap, analyzes leak chain

docs.title: Android Studio Memory Profiler
docs.text:
1. Run app in debuggable mode
2. Open Android Studio → Profiler
3. Click Memory section
4. Perform rotations, navigate, etc
5. Force garbage collection (GC button)
6. Inspect heap dump
7. Look for retained Activities

docs.title: Logcat Monitoring
docs.text:
adb logcat | grep -i "finalize"
adb logcat | grep -i "OutOfMemory"
adb logcat | grep -i "leak"

docs.title: Manual Detection (Monkey Testing)
docs.text:

// Watch memory in Profiler

docs.title: 1. Context Usage
docs.text:
// ✅ Use application context for singletons/long-lived objects
val context = applicationContext

// ❌ Don't store Activity context in singletons
companion object {
    var activity: Activity? = null  // WRONG
}

docs.title: 2. Static Inner Classes with WeakReference
docs.text:
// ✅ Correct pattern for holding Activity reference
private static class MyTask extends AsyncTask {
    private final WeakReference<MyActivity> activityRef;

    MyTask(MyActivity activity) {
        this.activityRef = new WeakReference<>(activity);
    }

    protected void onPostExecute(Result result) {
        MyActivity activity = activityRef.get();
        if (activity != null) {
            activity.updateUI(result);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 3. Always Unregister Listeners
docs.text:
override fun onResume() {
    super.onResume()
    eventBus.register(this)
}

override fun onPause() {
    eventBus.unregister(this)
    super.onPause()
}

docs.title: 4. Remove Handler Messages
docs.text:
override fun onDestroy() {
    handler.removeCallbacksAndMessages(null)
    super.onDestroy()
}

docs.title: 5. Use Lifecycle-Aware Components
docs.text:
// ✅ ViewModel + LiveData (auto lifecycle aware)
viewModel.data.observe(this) { data ->
    updateUI(data)
}

// ❌ Manual subscription (must unsubscribe)
subscription = dataSource.subscribe { data ->
    updateUI(data)
}
override fun onDestroy() {
    subscription.dispose()
}

docs.title: 6. Clean Up Binding References
docs.text:
private var binding: ActivityBinding? = null

override fun onDestroyView() {
    binding = null  // Null out binding
    super.onDestroyView()
}

docs.title: 7. Don't Pass Activity to Threads
docs.text:
// ❌ WRONG
Thread {
    val activity: Activity = this@MyActivity
    Thread.sleep(60000)
    activity.updateUI()
}.start()

// ✅ CORRECT: Use WeakReference
val threadSafe = Thread {
    val ref = WeakReference(this@MyActivity)
    Thread.sleep(60000)
    ref.get()?.updateUI()
}.apply { start() }

docs.title: Interview Knowledge
docs.text:
Q: What's the difference between OutOfMemoryError and memory leak? A: Memory leak = unused object still referenced (prevents GC) OOM = not enough memory left to allocate new objects Leaks cause OOM if allowed to accumulate

Q: Does assigning null prevent leaks? A: No, if object still referenced elsewhere, it's still a leak

Q: Why not always use WeakReference? A: Weak references can be GC'd at any time Use only when cleanup acceptable For critical objects, hold strong references

docs.text:
✅ Leak = unused object still referenced

✅ Common: Static refs, unregistered listeners, stored contexts

✅ LeakCanary = best tool for detection

✅ Use application context for long-lived objects

✅ Always unregister listeners/receivers in onDestroy()

✅ Use WeakReference for Activity references

✅ Remove Handler messages in onDestroy()

✅ Use ViewModel/LiveData instead of manual management

docs.title: Multitasking window focus
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Multitasking and Window Focus Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Modern Android supports split-screen, picture-in-picture, and rapid app switching. Lifecycle transitions depend on both visibility and input focus.

docs.title: Visibility vs Focus
docs.text:
• An activity can be visible but not focused.
  • Focus loss often triggers onPause().
  • Full invisibility transitions toward onStop().

docs.title: Split Screen
docs.text:
• Multiple activities may be visible.
  • Only one is primary focused for input at a time.

docs.title: Picture-in-Picture
docs.text:
• Host activity enters PiP mode.
  • Lifecycle and UI logic should adapt to reduced surface.

docs.title: App Switching
docs.text: • Foreground activity pauses/stops as another app resumes.

docs.title: Practical Handling
docs.text:
• Pause camera/mic/sensors in onPause() when appropriate.
  • Resume interaction-specific resources in onResume().
  • Persist transient UI state before potential stop/kill.

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• Equating visible with focused is incorrect.
  • Heavy cleanup in onPause() can degrade transitions.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Build lifecycle logic around visibility + focus, not only foreground/background.
  • Test on split-screen and PiP to validate assumptions.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Android permissions protect user data and sensitive device capabilities. Modern Android uses runtime permission prompts for dangerous permissions.

docs.title: Permission Categories
docs.text:
• Normal: auto-granted at install time.
  • Dangerous: runtime user consent required.
  • Signature: granted only to apps signed with same certificate.
  • Special: managed through settings screens (e.g., overlay).

docs.title: Runtime Permission Flow
docs.text:
private val requestCamera = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted ->
    if (granted) openCamera() else showPermissionRationaleOrFallback()
}

fun ensureCameraPermission() {
    when {
        ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA) ==
            PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> openCamera()
        shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) -> showRationale()
        else -> requestCamera.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
    }
}

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Ask only when feature is about to be used.
  • Explain user value clearly before prompt.
  • Gracefully degrade if denied.
  • Re-check permission before every sensitive action.

docs.title: Android Version Notes
docs.text:
• Android 6.0 introduced runtime model.
  • Scoped storage and media permissions evolved in Android 10+.
  • Android 13 split media permissions by type (READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, etc).

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Requesting many permissions at startup.
  • Assuming previously granted permissions remain granted forever.
  • Crashing on denial instead of fallback UX.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Permission handling is part of product UX, not just API usage.
  • Keep requests contextual, minimal, and reversible.
  • Always code for denial paths.

docs.title: Process death lifecycle
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Android can kill app processes under memory pressure. Robust apps restore state correctly when process is recreated.

docs.title: Lost on Process Death
docs.text:
• In-memory objects
  • ViewModel instances
  • Ongoing in-process jobs

docs.title: Can Be Restored
docs.text:
• savedInstanceState UI state
  • Persisted data from Room/files/preferences

docs.title: Recovery Pattern
docs.text:
1. Save lightweight UI state in onSaveInstanceState.
  2. Keep source of truth in persistent storage.
  3. Rehydrate screen state from repository on recreation.
override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
    outState.putInt("scroll", recyclerView.computeVerticalScrollOffset())
}

docs.title: Architecture Guidance
docs.text:
• UI state: Bundle + SavedStateHandle.
  • Durable state: Room/DataStore/network cache.
  • Avoid relying only on ViewModel for critical data.

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• "ViewModel survives process death" -> false.
  • Assuming onDestroy() always runs before death -> false.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Design for process death from day one.
  • Persist essentials and restore deterministically.

docs.title: Recyclerview efficiency
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: RecyclerView is efficient because it reuses view holders, minimizes view inflation, and delegates layout/animations to specialized components.

docs.title: Why RecyclerView Beats ListView
docs.text:
• ViewHolder pattern is first-class.
  • Better recycling and pooling.
  • Flexible LayoutManager implementations.
  • Built-in animation and diff-friendly update patterns.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
• RecyclerView
  • Adapter
  • ViewHolder
  • LayoutManager
  • Optional ItemAnimator and ItemDecoration

docs.title: Performance Practices
docs.text:
• Use ListAdapter + DiffUtil.
  • Keep onBindViewHolder() lightweight.
  • Avoid nested heavy layouts in item XML.
  • Use stable IDs when appropriate.
  • Pre-size image requests and cache aggressively.
class UserAdapter : ListAdapter<User, UserVH>(UserDiff()) {
    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): UserVH =
        UserVH(ItemUserBinding.inflate(LayoutInflater.from(parent.context), parent, false))

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: UserVH, position: Int) {
        holder.bind(getItem(position))
    }
}

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• Calling notifyDataSetChanged() too often hurts performance.
  • Doing expensive formatting or image decoding in bind causes jank.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• RecyclerView performance is mostly about efficient bind work and diffed updates.
  • Good item layout design matters as much as adapter logic.

docs.title: Rendering pipeline
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Android frame rendering follows a measure-layout-draw pipeline coordinated with display vsync. Missing frame deadlines causes jank.

docs.title: Frame Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Measure: determine view sizes.
  2. Layout: place views in parent bounds.
  3. Draw: record drawing commands.
  4. RenderThread/GPU: rasterize and compose.
  5. Display: present frame on next vsync.

docs.title: Frame Budget
docs.text:
• 60 Hz -> 16.67 ms per frame.
  • 120 Hz -> 8.33 ms per frame.
  • Exceeding budget drops/skips frames.

docs.title: Common Jank Sources
docs.text:
• Heavy work on main thread during input/animation.
  • Excessive layout passes (requestLayout storms).
  • Overdraw and complex alpha blending.
  • Expensive bitmap decode/transform at draw time.

docs.title: Optimization Strategies
docs.text:
• Flatten view hierarchies.
  • Avoid invalidating large areas unnecessarily.
  • Precompute text/layout data.
  • Move expensive work off main thread.
  • Use profiler tools to target hotspots.

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• "GPU accelerated" does not mean main thread can block.
  • Smoothness requires both CPU and GPU staying within frame budget.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Rendering performance is deadline-driven.
  • Measure, profile, then optimize the true bottleneck.

docs.title: Services
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A Service is an Android component used for background work that should continue independently of UI screens. Services do not provide UI and are managed by the system with their own lifecycle.

docs.title: Started Service
docs.text:
• Started with startService() or startForegroundService().
  • Runs until stopSelf()/stopService() is called.
  • Good for one-off background tasks.

docs.title: Bound Service
docs.text:
• Started with bindService().
  • Exposes APIs via IBinder.
  • Runs while clients are bound (unless also started).
  • Useful for in-process or cross-process IPC.

docs.title: Foreground Service
docs.text:
• Must show persistent notification.
  • Higher priority, less likely to be killed.
  • Required for user-visible long-running tasks.

docs.title: Started Service Flow
docs.text:
override fun onCreate() {
    super.onCreate()
}

override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
    // Do work off main thread
    return START_NOT_STICKY
}

override fun onDestroy() {
    super.onDestroy()
}

docs.title: Restart Modes
docs.text:
• START_NOT_STICKY: Do not recreate after kill.
  • START_STICKY: Recreate service, intent may be null.
  • START_REDELIVER_INTENT: Recreate and redeliver last intent.

docs.title: Service vs Thread
docs.text:
• Thread: execution unit, tied to process lifetime.
  • Service: component managed by Android lifecycle.
  • Service work still needs threading (Dispatchers.IO, Executor, etc).

docs.title: Bound Service Example
docs.text:
class PlayerService : Service() {
    private val binder = LocalBinder()

    inner class LocalBinder : Binder() {
        fun getService(): PlayerService = this@PlayerService
    }

    override fun onBind(intent: Intent?): IBinder = binder

    fun play(trackId: String) {
        // business logic
    }
}

private val connection = object : ServiceConnection {
    override fun onServiceConnected(name: ComponentName?, service: IBinder?) {
        val binder = service as PlayerService.LocalBinder
        val playerService = binder.getService()
        playerService.play("track_1")
    }

    override fun onServiceDisconnected(name: ComponentName?) = Unit
}

docs.title: Android 8+ Background Limits
docs.text:
• Background service starts are restricted.
  • Use startForegroundService() when required.
  • Prefer WorkManager for deferrable background work.

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• Service does not run on a separate thread by default.
  • Foreground service requires notification promptly.
  • IntentService is deprecated; use WorkManager.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Services represent background-capable components, not threading primitives.
  • Choose started, bound, or foreground based on interaction and visibility.
  • Use modern background APIs (WorkManager) for resilient scheduling.

docs.title: Storage types
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Android offers multiple storage options with different security, structure, and sharing behavior. Choosing the right one is a common interview topic.

docs.title: SharedPreferences / DataStore
docs.text:
• Key-value preferences.
  • Best for flags/settings.
  • For modern apps, prefer DataStore over legacy preferences APIs.

docs.title: Internal Storage
docs.text:
• App-private files.
  • Removed on uninstall.
  • Good for private cached or persisted files.

docs.title: External/Scoped Storage
docs.text:
• Shared media/documents model.
  • Scoped storage rules apply on modern Android.
  • Use MediaStore / SAF depending on use case.

docs.title: Room/SQLite
docs.text:
• Structured relational data.
  • Queryable and transactional.
  • Best for offline-first and complex domain models.

docs.title: Cache Directories
docs.text:
• Temporary, reclaimable by system.
  • Never store critical data only in cache.

docs.title: Selection Guide
docs.text:
• Settings -> DataStore/SharedPreferences
  • Structured domain data -> Room
  • User-visible media -> MediaStore
  • Temporary payloads -> Cache

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• Assuming external storage is always globally readable/writable.
  • Storing large structured data in preferences.
  • Ignoring migration/backup strategy.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Match storage choice to data lifetime and access pattern.
  • Prefer modern APIs (Room, DataStore, scoped media APIs).

docs.title: Task and backstack
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Task and Back Stack Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: A task is a collection of activities arranged in a back stack. Back navigation pops activities in LIFO order and task/intent flags can significantly change behavior.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Task: logical user journey container.
  • Back stack: activity stack inside task.
  • Recents screen: task-level entry point.

docs.title: Launch and Back Behavior
docs.text:
• New activity usually pushed to current task stack.
  • Back pops top activity.
  • If root popped, task leaves foreground.

docs.title: Important Flags
docs.text:
• FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK: launch in new or existing task by affinity.
  • FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP: pop above target if already in stack.
  • FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP: reuse top instance via onNewIntent().

docs.title: Launch Modes (high level)
docs.text:
• standard
  • singleTop
  • singleTask
  • singleInstance / singleInstancePerTask

Use sparingly; prefer Navigation Component defaults unless specific behavior needed.

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• Mixing launch modes and flags can create unexpected UX.
  • Deep links may create parallel task flows if misconfigured.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Understand default stack behavior first, then add flags intentionally.
  • Validate navigation with real back/recents testing.

docs.title: Zygote process creation
docs.text: ← Back to Fundamentals

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Zygote is a special Android process that preloads framework/runtime state and forks app processes quickly, reducing cold start overhead.

docs.title: Why Zygote Exists
docs.text:
• Starting a fresh VM per app is expensive.
  • Preloading classes/resources once and forking is faster.
  • Copy-on-write allows shared memory pages until modified.

docs.title: Process Creation Flow
docs.text:
1. System boots and starts Zygote.
  2. Zygote preloads framework classes/resources.
  3. ActivityManager requests new app process.
  4. Zygote fork() creates child process.
  5. Child process initializes app runtime and Application.

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text:
• Faster app startup, especially cold start.
  • Better memory sharing across app processes.

docs.title: Interview Traps
docs.text:
• Zygote does not run your app code directly; child process does.
  • Forked process still performs app-specific initialization.
  • Process creation speed depends on more than Zygote (I/O, app init work).

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Zygote is central to Android startup architecture.
  • Fork + copy-on-write is core optimization.
  • Keep app initialization lean to benefit fully.

docs.title: Cancellation and exception handling
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Cancellation and Exception Handling Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Cancellation and exception propagation are where coroutine understanding becomes production-relevant.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text: Coroutine cancellation is cooperative. It works well when code reaches suspension points or checks cancellation explicitly.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Exception behavior depends on:

  • coroutine builder (launch vs async)
  • parent-child hierarchy
  • supervisor boundaries
  • where exceptions are observed

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Cancellation is represented by job state changes and propagated through job hierarchy.

A coroutine that never suspends or checks cancellation may continue running longer than expected.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Suspend functions cooperate with cancellation through coroutine machinery, not through thread interruption alone.

CoroutineExceptionHandler is only for uncaught exceptions; it is not a general substitute for structured error handling.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
while (isActive) {
    doWorkChunk()
}

try {
    doWork()
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is cancellation called cooperative?
  • Why should CancellationException usually be rethrown?
  • Why doesn't CoroutineExceptionHandler catch everything?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Common bugs:

  • swallowing cancellation accidentally
  • blocking threads inside coroutines
  • assuming try/catch and handler behavior are identical across builders

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Cancellation responsiveness matters for UI, battery, and resource cleanup. Poor cancellation behavior can waste work and degrade UX.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Good coroutine engineers think about cancellation and exception strategy during API design, not only when debugging failures.

docs.title: Collections and sequences
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kotlin collections are highly expressive, but interview discussions often focus on eagerness, allocation behavior, and immutability semantics.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Common operations:

  • map
  • filter
  • flatMap
  • groupBy
  • associate

Key nuance:

  • List<T> is read-only from that API surface
  • it is not necessarily deeply immutable

Sequences differ because they are lazy.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Collection chains usually allocate intermediate collections. Sequence chains defer work and process lazily.

That means sequences can reduce allocations, but also add iterator/lazy overhead.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: The compiler does not magically optimize every chain away. Standard library operations still correspond to loops, lambdas, and allocated containers depending on API choice.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val names = users
    .filter { it.active }
    .map { it.name }

val names = users.asSequence()
    .filter { it.active }
    .map { it.name }
    .toList()

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When should you use Sequence?
  • Are Kotlin collections immutable?
  • Why can operator chains become allocation-heavy?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Use collection chains for readable business logic. Switch to sequences only when dataset size and allocation pressure justify it.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
• small collections: eager collections are often fine
  • large pipelines: sequences may help
  • hot paths: benchmark rather than assume

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong answers avoid blanket rules like “Sequence is always faster.” Context matters.

docs.title: Coroutines foundations
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kotlin coroutines provide a structured, lightweight way to write asynchronous code in a sequential style.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Core building blocks:

  • suspend functions
  • CoroutineScope
  • CoroutineContext
  • Job
  • Dispatcher

Coroutines are not threads. They are units of work scheduled onto threads.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Suspend functions compile into continuation-passing style. The compiler transforms suspend code into resumable state machines.

At a high level, the transformation adds:

  • a continuation parameter
  • labels/states
  • logic for resuming from suspension points

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
A suspend function is not just “async syntax.” It becomes lower-level machinery that coordinates with Continuation objects and resumable state transitions.

This is one of the most important advanced Kotlin interview topics.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
suspend fun fetchUser(): User {
    delay(100)
    return User("1")
}

Conceptually, the compiler rewrites this into a resumable form rather than a simple blocking method.

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Does suspend mean background thread?
  • What is a continuation?
  • How are coroutines lighter than threads?
  • What does CPS transformation mean?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Coroutines simplify async logic, but misuse can still cause:

  • lifecycle leaks
  • wrong dispatcher use
  • hidden cancellation bugs
  • unstructured work

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Coroutines are cheaper than threads, but not free. Large numbers of coroutines still create scheduling and allocation overhead.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
The strongest interview answers explain coroutines at both levels:

  • high-level developer ergonomics
  • low-level compiler/runtime model

docs.title: Data classes and generated code
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Data Classes and Generated Code Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Data classes are Kotlin's value-oriented modeling tool. They remove boilerplate while making equality, debugging, and copying semantics explicit.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
A data class is best when the object primarily represents data rather than identity-heavy behavior.

data class User(
    val id: Long,
    val name: String
)

Kotlin generates:

  • equals()
  • hashCode()
  • toString()
  • copy()
  • componentN()

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
The compiler only uses properties in the primary constructor for generated member behavior.

data class Session(val token: String) {
    var isExpired: Boolean = false
}

Here:

  • token participates in equality/hash/copy
  • isExpired does not

That is an important interview trap.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Kotlin data classes compile to normal JVM classes with generated methods.

Conceptually, the compiler emits methods similar to:

override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean
override fun hashCode(): Int
override fun toString(): String
fun copy(id: Long = this.id, name: String = this.name): User
operator fun component1(): Long
operator fun component2(): String

Default arguments in copy() also generate additional helper methods on JVM.

docs.title: Copying immutable state
docs.text:
data class UiState(
    val loading: Boolean,
    val title: String
)

val oldState = UiState(loading = true, title = "Home")
val newState = oldState.copy(loading = false)

docs.title: Destructuring
docs.text:
val user = User(1L, "Mina")
val (id, name) = user

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What gets included in generated equality?
  • Is a data class automatically immutable?
  • Why is copy() useful in Android UI state?
  • When should you avoid data classes?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use data classes for:

  • UI state
  • API models
  • cached domain values
  • immutable state containers

Avoid overusing them for objects with strong identity/lifecycle semantics.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Data classes are usually efficient enough, but beware of:

  • repeated copy() on large nested graphs
  • accidental deep-state churn in UI reducers
  • large generated toString() logs in hot paths

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
The strongest interview answers distinguish:

  • value semantics vs identity semantics
  • generated convenience vs real allocation cost
  • immutable state modeling vs mutable entities

That distinction matters heavily in Android architecture and state management.

docs.title: Delegation and delegated properties
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Delegation and Delegated Properties Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Delegation is one of Kotlin's strongest language features for reducing boilerplate and favoring composition.

docs.title: Class delegation
docs.text:
interface Printer {
    fun print()
}

class ConsolePrinter : Printer {
    override fun print() = println("print")
}

class Screen(printer: Printer) : Printer by printer

This forwards interface implementation automatically.

docs.title: Property delegation
docs.text:
val config by lazy { loadConfig() }

The delegate owns access behavior.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Delegated properties are compiled into calls to delegate operators such as:

  • getValue()
  • setValue()

Class delegation similarly becomes generated forwarding methods.

So Kotlin removes boilerplate, but the underlying implementation still uses regular method calls and generated glue.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
lazy uses a delegate implementation chosen by thread-safety mode.

Common modes:

  • synchronized (default)
  • publication
  • none

This matters in interview discussions because “lazy” behavior is not one-size-fits-all.

docs.title: lazy
docs.text:
val repository by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) {
    UserRepository()
}

docs.title: Observable property
docs.text:
var count: Int by Delegates.observable(0) { _, old, new ->
    println("$old -> $new")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is delegation better than inheritance here?
  • How does lazy behave with threads?
  • What methods must a custom delegate implement?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Delegation is excellent for:

  • reusable behaviors
  • view binding style patterns
  • state observation
  • lightweight wrappers

But hidden magic can hurt readability if overused.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Delegation reduces manual boilerplate but still introduces generated calls. In most app code the clarity benefit outweighs the tiny indirection cost.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong candidates explain delegation as a language-supported composition mechanism, not just “syntactic sugar.” That distinction matters in architecture discussions.

docs.title: Dispatchers and coroutine scope
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Dispatchers and Coroutine Scope Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Dispatchers and scopes determine where coroutines run and who owns their lifetime.

docs.title: Dispatchers
docs.text:
• Main → UI thread
  • IO → blocking I/O work
  • Default → CPU-heavy work
  • Unconfined → special-case behavior, rarely appropriate in app code

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text: A CoroutineScope defines the lifecycle boundary for its coroutines.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Dispatchers are elements of coroutine context. Scopes combine context plus job hierarchy rules.

The important concept is that execution context and ownership travel together through coroutine context composition.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Dispatchers do not change what coroutines are. They change scheduling and thread execution behavior.

withContext(...) is commonly used to switch execution context safely.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
viewModelScope.launch {
    val result = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        repository.fetch()
    }
    render(result)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What is the difference between scope and dispatcher?
  • Why is Dispatchers.IO different from Default?
  • Why is GlobalScope discouraged?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use lifecycle-aware scopes on Android:

  • viewModelScope
  • lifecycleScope

Avoid unowned coroutine launches unless there is a very explicit reason.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Wrong dispatcher selection can cause:

  • blocked UI
  • thread starvation
  • wasted parallelism
  • poor responsiveness

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level answers connect dispatcher choice to workload type and connect scope choice to ownership and cancellation boundaries.

docs.title: Extension functions
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Extension functions make Kotlin APIs feel richer without modifying original classes.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
fun String.firstCharOrNull(): Char? = firstOrNull()

This reads like a member call:

val c = "Kotlin".firstCharOrNull()

But extension functions do not actually inject members into the class.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Extensions are compiled as static-like functions with the receiver passed as an argument.

That is why extension dispatch is static, not virtual.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Key interview rules:

  • receiver is just a parameter at compile time
  • member functions beat extensions if signatures match
  • runtime subtype does not change extension resolution
open class A
class B : A()

fun A.label() = "A"
fun B.label() = "B"

val value: A = B()
println(value.label()) // "A"

docs.title: Android-flavored helper
docs.text:
fun TextView.showIf(condition: Boolean) {
    visibility = if (condition) View.VISIBLE else View.GONE
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Are extension functions polymorphic?
  • Do they really modify the original class?
  • When should you prefer extension functions over utility objects?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use extensions for:

  • readable helpers
  • framework convenience APIs
  • DSL-like builders

Avoid putting too much business logic in obscure extension files.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Extensions usually have no special runtime magic beyond regular function calls unless combined with inline.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Extension functions are great API design tools, but poor organization can make code discovery harder. Keep naming and file placement disciplined.

docs.title: Flow fundamentals
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Flow is Kotlin's coroutine-based asynchronous stream API and a core part of modern Android data pipelines.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Key properties of Flow:

  • cold by default
  • sequential by default
  • cancellation-aware
  • coroutine based

A cold stream starts producing values for each collector independently.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
A flow builder defines a suspendable emission pipeline. Collection triggers execution.

That means a Flow is closer to a reusable recipe for producing values than a constantly running producer.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: Flow sits on top of coroutines and suspend machinery. Many operators are implemented as chains of suspendable transformations.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
fun userFlow(): Flow<User> = flow {
    emit(loadUser())
}

viewModelScope.launch {
    userFlow().collect { user ->
        render(user)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What does “cold” mean in Flow?
  • How is Flow different from LiveData or Rx streams?
  • Why is Flow sequential by default?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Flow is powerful for:

  • repository streams
  • UI state pipelines
  • database observation
  • combining async sources

But careless operator chains and repeated collections can create inefficiency.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Understand:

  • collection triggers execution
  • repeated collectors repeat cold work
  • buffering/concurrency operators affect throughput and ordering

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: The strongest answers explain Flow not just as “reactive streams,” but as coroutine-native cold stream pipelines with explicit lifecycle and collection semantics.

docs.title: Generics and variance
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kotlin generics improve type safety, but their most important interview topics are variance and type erasure.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Generics let APIs work across different types safely:

class Box<T>(val value: T)

Variance controls subtype relationships:

  • out = producer
  • in = consumer

Star projection (*) represents an unknown type argument safely.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
On JVM, generic type arguments are largely erased at runtime. That means many generic guarantees exist mainly at compile time.

This is why runtime checks and reified solutions matter.

docs.title: Covariance
docs.text: interface Source<out T>

docs.title: Contravariance
docs.text: interface Consumer<in T>

docs.title: Star projection
docs.text:
val list: List<*> = listOf("a", "b")

Kotlin avoids Java-style raw type ambiguity by making unknown generic usage safer.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
fun copyAll(from: List<out Number>, to: MutableList<in Number>) {
    from.forEach { to.add(it) }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What is variance?
  • What is the producer/consumer rule?
  • Why does type erasure matter?
  • Why is List<String> not automatically List<Any>?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Variance improves API correctness, especially in libraries and architecture boundaries. Poor variance choices can make APIs painful or unsafe.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The main cost is not performance but complexity. The challenge is making APIs type-safe without making them unreadable.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Strong answers connect generic theory to real API design:

  • safe library surfaces
  • better abstraction boundaries
  • reduced casting
  • more predictable contracts

docs.title: Higher order functions and lambdas
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Higher-Order Functions and Lambdas Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Higher-order functions are central to idiomatic Kotlin API design. They power collection transformations, builders, coroutines, Flow, and DSLs.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
A higher-order function either:

  • accepts a function
  • returns a function
fun repeat(times: Int, block: () -> Unit) {
    kotlin.repeat(times) { block() }
}

Lambda with receiver example:

fun buildMessage(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String {
    return StringBuilder().apply(block).toString()
}

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Lambdas can compile into:

  • generated classes/objects
  • inlined code when used with inline functions

Lambdas with receiver are still function types, but with an implicit receiver available inside the body.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Without inlining, lambdas may allocate objects. With inline functions, the compiler can reduce or remove that overhead.

This is why Kotlin's higher-order style is expressive but still tied to JVM allocation and bytecode tradeoffs.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val doubled = listOf(1, 2, 3).map { it * 2 }

val text = buildMessage {
    append("Hello ")
    append("Kotlin")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why are higher-order functions important in Kotlin?
  • What is a lambda with receiver?
  • How do inline functions affect lambda cost?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Use higher-order APIs to improve abstraction and reuse, but avoid creating APIs so abstract that they become hard to debug.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Main cost areas:

  • lambda allocation
  • capturing outer variables
  • deep operator chains

These matter most in hot paths.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: The best Kotlin APIs often feel declarative because of higher-order functions, but strong engineers balance API elegance with debuggability and runtime cost.

docs.title: Inline functions
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Inline functions are a compiler-level optimization and language feature used heavily with Kotlin lambdas and reified generics.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
inline fun measure(block: () -> Unit) {
    val start = System.nanoTime()
    block()
    println(System.nanoTime() - start)
}

Inlining means the function body may be copied into the call site.

Benefits:

  • fewer lambda allocations
  • fewer function call boundaries
  • support for non-local returns in inline lambdas

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
The compiler substitutes the inline function body directly into call sites when possible.

This is why:

  • reified type parameters work
  • non-local returns become possible
  • bytecode can grow if abused

docs.title: noinline
docs.text: Prevents a specific lambda from being inlined.

docs.title: crossinline
docs.text:
Allows inlining but forbids non-local return.

These exist because not all lambda usages can be inlined safely or semantically.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
inline fun runner(block: () -> Unit) {
    block()
}

inline fun wrapper(crossinline block: () -> Unit) {
    val r = Runnable { block() }
    r.run()
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why are inline functions useful for higher-order APIs?
  • When do they hurt performance?
  • Why does reified require inline?
  • What do crossinline and noinline solve?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Inline small, hot higher-order utilities. Avoid inlining large bodies blindly.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Inlining can remove overhead, but can also increase:

  • bytecode size
  • method complexity
  • instruction cache pressure

It is a targeted optimization, not a blanket rule.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Good interview answers connect inline functions to:

  • bytecode tradeoffs
  • lambda allocation behavior
  • API ergonomics
  • reified generics support

docs.title: Jvm interop and bytecode
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: JVM Interop and Bytecode Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Kotlin is deeply integrated with the JVM. Understanding interop and bytecode helps explain how Kotlin features behave in real Android codebases.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Important interop topics:

  • calling Java from Kotlin
  • exposing Kotlin to Java
  • nullability differences
  • default arguments
  • companion/static-like APIs
  • SAM conversions

Important bytecode topics:

  • generated helper methods
  • lambda classes
  • null checks
  • suspend state machines
  • inline expansion

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Many Kotlin features are compiler conveniences over regular JVM structures.

Examples:

  • default arguments generate helper methods
  • top-level declarations compile into generated holder classes
  • suspend functions add continuation machinery

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Kotlin source can look very high-level, but the emitted bytecode still follows JVM constraints.

That is why knowledge of:

  • type erasure
  • generated methods
  • interop annotations
  • bytecode layout

makes interview answers much stronger.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
class UserFactory {
    companion object {
        @JvmStatic
        fun create() = UserFactory()
    }
}

inline fun <reified T> check(value: Any) = value is T

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How does Kotlin handle Java nullability?
  • What does @JvmStatic do?
  • Why does Kotlin generate extra methods?
  • How do suspend functions appear in bytecode?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Interop bugs often happen at boundaries:

  • Java APIs with unclear nullability
  • default args exposed poorly to Java
  • reflection/serialization expectations
  • method count and generated helper complexity

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Bytecode awareness helps explain:

  • method growth
  • allocation behavior
  • lambda overhead
  • inlining tradeoffs

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior candidates stand out when they connect Kotlin language ergonomics to emitted JVM artifacts and operational consequences.

docs.title: Kotlin basics
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Kotlin is a modern statically typed language that runs primarily on the JVM and was designed to improve safety, expressiveness, and developer productivity.

For Android interviews, Kotlin basics are not just syntax questions. Interviewers often expect you to connect Kotlin language design to:

  • safer APIs
  • fewer runtime crashes
  • clearer state modeling
  • better interop with Java
  • reduced boilerplate in Android apps

docs.title: Why Kotlin became the Android default
docs.text:
Kotlin fits Android well because it improves several pain points from Java-heavy Android codebases:

  • null handling is explicit in the type system
  • common patterns require less code
  • lambdas and extension functions make APIs cleaner
  • coroutines improve async programming ergonomics
  • interoperability lets teams adopt it incrementally

docs.title: val vs var
docs.text:
val name = "Kotlin"
var count = 0
  • val = reference cannot be reassigned
  • var = reference can be reassigned

Important nuance:

val items = mutableListOf("a")
items.add("b") // valid
// items = mutableListOf() // invalid

So val gives a stable reference, not automatic deep immutability.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
From a compiler perspective, Kotlin basics still map to regular JVM concepts:

  • top-level functions become static-like methods in generated classes
  • properties compile into fields/getters/setters depending on usage
  • val often becomes a field with getter only
  • var usually becomes a field with both getter and setter

The surface syntax is cleaner, but the generated model is still understandable from a JVM point of view.

docs.title: Property generation
docs.text:
class User {
    val id: Int = 1
    var name: String = "A"
}

This generally compiles into:

  • backing fields when needed
  • getId()
  • getName()
  • setName()

Interview insight: Kotlin language features often look new, but many are compiler conveniences over classic bytecode patterns.

docs.title: Prefer val by default
docs.text:
val repository = UserRepository()
val users = repository.loadUsers()

docs.title: Use var only when mutation is real and local
docs.text:
var retries = 0
while (retries < 3) {
    retries++
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is val preferred over var?
  • Does val mean immutable object?
  • What does Kotlin compile to on the JVM?
  • Why is Kotlin safer than Java in practice?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• prefer immutable modeling for UI state
  • keep mutation local and obvious
  • use Kotlin features to improve maintainability, not cleverness
  • avoid excessive nesting of idiomatic helpers if readability drops

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Basic Kotlin syntax itself is not usually the bottleneck.

The real performance questions come from:

  • allocation patterns
  • lambdas and closures
  • inlining
  • collection transformations
  • coroutine usage

So Kotlin basics matter more for correctness and readability than raw speed.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Strong Kotlin interview answers connect language fundamentals to engineering tradeoffs:

  • val improves reasoning about state
  • explicit nullability improves API contracts
  • better syntax can reduce bug surface area
  • compiler-generated convenience still has JVM cost and structure

The best answers show both language fluency and runtime awareness.

docs.title: Null safety and smart casts
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Null Safety and Smart Casts Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Null safety is one of Kotlin's biggest value propositions. It moves many null-related problems from runtime into the type system.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Kotlin distinguishes:

  • String → non-nullable
  • String? → nullable

Main tools:

  • safe call ?.
  • Elvis ?:
  • not-null assertion !!
  • smart casts after checks

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Kotlin null safety is mostly compiler enforced. The type system tracks nullable vs non-nullable references and emits checks where needed.

Platform types from Java weaken these guarantees because nullability may be unknown at compile time.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
The compiler often inserts runtime null-checks for parameters and assumptions, especially around Java interop and non-null contracts.

Smart casts rely on flow analysis. They work only when the compiler can prove the reference is stable.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val name: String? = input()
val length = name?.length ?: 0

if (value is String) {
    println(value.length) // smart cast
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why can null still happen in Kotlin?
  • What is a platform type?
  • When do smart casts fail?
  • Why is !! dangerous?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid !! unless failure is intentional
  • make nullability explicit in public APIs
  • be careful at Java boundaries
  • prefer safe transformations to assertions

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Null safety is primarily a correctness feature. Runtime cost is usually minor compared with the stability benefit.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Good candidates explain that Kotlin reduces null problems significantly, but cannot eliminate them when unsafe assertions, Java interop, reflection, or poor API design are involved.

docs.title: Object and companion objects
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Object and Companion Objects Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text:
Kotlin's object keyword covers several patterns:

  • singleton declarations
  • anonymous object expressions
  • companion objects

Interviewers often test whether you understand both the syntax and the runtime differences.

docs.title: Object declaration
docs.text:
object Logger {
    fun log(message: String) = println(message)
}
  • named singleton
  • lazily initialized on first access
  • useful for stateless shared utilities

docs.title: Object expression
docs.text:
val listener = object : Runnable {
    override fun run() = println("run")
}
  • anonymous object
  • created immediately
  • often used for local callbacks

docs.title: Companion object
docs.text:
class User {
    companion object {
        const val TABLE = "users"
    }
}
  • tied to a class
  • often used for factories/constants
  • Kotlin alternative to many Java static use cases

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Companion objects are still real objects. They are not magical static blocks.

That means they can:

  • implement interfaces
  • hold state
  • contain functions
  • be referenced as objects
class FactoryHolder {
    companion object Factory : Comparator<Int> {
        override fun compare(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a - b
    }
}

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
On JVM, Kotlin often generates a companion instance field plus methods.

With annotations like @JvmStatic, interop can become more Java-friendly.

Interview nuance:

  • companion objects are object instances
  • Java statics are class-level members
  • the call style may look similar, but the compiled model differs

docs.title: Factory pattern
docs.text:
class User private constructor(val id: Long) {
    companion object {
        fun fromId(id: Long): User = User(id)
    }
}

docs.title: Anonymous object for one-off behavior
docs.text:
fun makeRunnable(): Runnable {
    return object : Runnable {
        override fun run() = println("working")
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Is a companion object the same as static?
  • When is an object declaration initialized?
  • What is lost when returning an anonymous object from a public API?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use object declarations for:

  • stateless helpers
  • shared formatters
  • singleton configuration readers

Avoid hidden global mutable state unless truly necessary.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The main concern is usually not speed but initialization and hidden state. Singleton misuse can quietly turn into global coupling.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Strong answers emphasize:

  • object forms model different intent
  • companion objects are still objects
  • singletons simplify access but can hurt testability if overused

docs.title: Reified generics
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Reified generics are one of Kotlin's most interview-worthy features because they connect language syntax to JVM type erasure and compiler inlining.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Normally, JVM generics are erased at runtime.

Kotlin solves some of that limitation with reified type parameters in inline functions:

inline fun <reified T> Any.isType(): Boolean = this is T

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Because the function is inlined, the compiler can substitute real type checks at the call site.

That is why this is possible only inside inline functions.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Without reified support, this is not possible safely:

fun <T> check(value: Any): Boolean {
    // cannot use `is T` here normally
    return false
}

With reified:

inline fun <reified T> check(value: Any): Boolean = value is T

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJsonTyped(json: String): T {
    return fromJson(json, T::class.java)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why does reified require inline?
  • How does it relate to type erasure?
  • When is reified more useful than reflection?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Reified generics improve API ergonomics, but still depend on JVM/runtime limits. They are especially useful for utility libraries and framework helpers.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The main tradeoff is still inline-related bytecode duplication, not magic runtime cost.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong answers connect reified generics to compiler substitution, not just “Kotlin can access generic types at runtime.” The mechanism matters.

docs.title: Scope functions
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Scope functions help structure object-centric code, but their real interview value is understanding tradeoffs, not memorizing a chart.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Main functions:

  • let
  • run
  • with
  • apply
  • also

They differ by:

  • receiver style (this vs it)
  • return type (receiver vs lambda result)

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text: Scope functions are just normal library functions. There is no special runtime scope feature; readability comes from how the compiler resolves receivers and lambda parameters.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: At bytecode level, these become regular function calls/lambda invocations. The complexity is mainly cognitive, not magical.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val length = name?.let { it.trim().length }

val user = User().apply {
    id = 1
    name = "Mina"
}

logger.also {
    println("created")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Which scope function returns the receiver?
  • Which one is best for null-safe transforms?
  • Why can overusing scope functions hurt readability?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Good uses:

  • object setup with apply
  • null-safe transforms with let
  • side-effect logging with also

Bad uses:

  • deeply nested chained scopes
  • mixing multiple implicit receivers carelessly

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Performance differences are usually minor. Readability and maintainability matter more.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior engineers choose scope functions intentionally. The best code often uses fewer of them, not more.

docs.title: Sealed classes and enums
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Sealed Classes and Enums Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Sealed classes and enum classes both model limited domains, but they solve different problems.

docs.title: Enum classes
docs.text:
Best for a fixed set of singleton constants.

enum class SortOrder {
    ASCENDING,
    DESCENDING
}

docs.title: Sealed classes
docs.text:
Best for closed hierarchies where each case may carry different data.

sealed class UiState {
    object Loading : UiState()
    data class Success(val items: List<String>) : UiState()
    data class Error(val message: String) : UiState()
}

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Enums create one instance per enum constant. Sealed classes define a restricted inheritance tree.

Key difference:

  • enum = fixed constants
  • sealed = fixed subtype set

That makes sealed classes much stronger for state/result/event modeling.

docs.title: Enums
docs.text: Compile to Java-style enum classes with constant instances.

docs.title: Sealed classes
docs.text:
Compile as regular classes/interfaces with metadata allowing the compiler to reason about exhaustiveness.

The JVM itself does not “understand” sealed behavior the same way Kotlin source does; much of the experience is compiler driven.

docs.title: Exhaustive when
docs.text:
fun render(state: UiState): String = when (state) {
    UiState.Loading -> "loading"
    is UiState.Success -> state.items.joinToString()
    is UiState.Error -> state.message
}

docs.title: Enum use case
docs.text:
enum class ThemeMode {
    LIGHT,
    DARK,
    SYSTEM
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When should you choose sealed over enum?
  • Why is sealed useful for UI state?
  • Does sealed always mean no else in when?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use enums for:

  • simple flags
  • static modes
  • limited status values

Use sealed classes for:

  • state machines
  • result wrappers
  • navigation outcomes
  • view state models

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The choice is usually more about modeling clarity than raw performance. But sealed class instances can allocate more frequently if used carelessly in high-frequency state updates.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
The best modeling tool is the one that matches the domain:

  • enum for simple symbolic constants
  • sealed for structured closed-state systems

That distinction improves both correctness and maintainability.

docs.title: Stateflow sharedflow and channels
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: StateFlow, SharedFlow, and Channels Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: These primitives solve different streaming and coordination problems in coroutine-based systems.

docs.title: StateFlow
docs.text:
• always has a current value
  • best for state exposure
  • good for UI state models

docs.title: SharedFlow
docs.text:
• hot broadcast stream
  • configurable replay/buffering
  • good for events/shared emissions

docs.title: Channel
docs.text:
• point-to-point communication primitive
  • queue-like semantics
  • send/receive model

docs.title: Mutex
docs.text:
• protects shared mutable state cooperatively
  • suspends instead of blocking threads

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
These primitives differ in ownership and delivery semantics:

  • state retention (StateFlow)
  • broadcast fan-out (SharedFlow)
  • queue handoff (Channel)
  • mutual exclusion (Mutex)

Interviewers often care more about correct use-case matching than API memorization.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: All of them are coroutine/runtime constructs, not magical language features. Their behavior emerges from concurrency contracts and buffering rules.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state

private val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>()

val mutex = Mutex()
mutex.withLock {
    updateSharedState()
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• StateFlow vs SharedFlow?
  • Channel vs SharedFlow?
  • When use Mutex instead of synchronized locking?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Common mistakes:

  • using StateFlow for one-off UI events
  • using channels where broadcast behavior is needed
  • ignoring replay/buffer semantics
  • mutating shared state without synchronization

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Hot stream choice affects:

  • memory retention
  • buffering pressure
  • event loss or duplication
  • collector coordination cost

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong engineers choose these primitives based on delivery semantics and lifecycle guarantees, not habit.

docs.title: Structured concurrency and jobs
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Structured Concurrency and Jobs Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Structured concurrency gives coroutine trees clear ownership and predictable lifecycle behavior.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
In structured concurrency:

  • coroutines are launched in a scope
  • parent-child relationships are explicit
  • parents usually wait for children
  • cancellation and failure have defined propagation rules

Job represents coroutine lifecycle. SupervisorJob changes failure propagation semantics.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Each coroutine context usually includes a Job element. Child jobs attach to parent jobs to build a hierarchy.

This hierarchy powers:

  • cancellation propagation
  • completion coordination
  • structured waiting

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
This is not just syntax style. The runtime job tree controls actual coroutine lifecycle behavior.

That is why launch, async, Job, and SupervisorJob matter beyond API surface.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
coroutineScope {
    launch { workA() }
    launch { workB() }
}

val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main)

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is structured concurrency safer than ad-hoc launching?
  • What is the difference between Job and SupervisorJob?
  • When should you use async instead of launch?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use structured concurrency to avoid:

  • leaked work
  • orphan background jobs
  • unpredictable cancellation behavior

This is especially important in Android lifecycle-bound scopes.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Structured concurrency is mainly about correctness and maintainability, but it also improves debuggability and reduces accidental runaway work.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: The best answers explain job hierarchy as an ownership model, not just an API detail. That framing is what interviewers often want.

docs.title: What is MVVM in Android architecture?
docs.text:
beginner architecture mvvm android View Answer

MVVM separates UI rendering from business/data orchestration.

Typical split:

  • View: renders state and forwards user actions
  • ViewModel: exposes lifecycle-aware UI state

Why teams use it:

  • better testability
  • cleaner separation of concerns
  • easier lifecycle-safe state handling

docs.title: What is the role of a ViewModel in scalable Android apps?
docs.text:
beginner architecture viewmodel state View Answer

ViewModel owns screen-level state and survives configuration changes.

Key responsibilities:

  • transform domain data into UI-friendly state
  • coordinate use cases/repositories
  • expose immutable observable state
  • handle user intents/events

It should avoid direct Android UI references.

docs.title: When should you use SavedStateHandle in architecture design?

intermediate architecture viewmodel state View Answer

docs.title: What is MVI architecture?
docs.text:
intermediate architecture mvi state View Answer

MVI models UI as a loop: intent -> reducer -> new immutable state.

  • easier debugging/time-travel style reasoning

docs.title: MVVM vs MVI - how do you choose?
docs.text:
senior architecture mvvm mvi View Answer

Choose by complexity and team needs, not trend preference.

MVVM:

  • lower ceremony
  • common Android default

docs.title: What is the Activity Lifecycle?
docs.text:
beginner android lifecycle fundamentals View Answer

The Activity Lifecycle is the sequence of states an Android Activity transitions through from creation to destruction.

Android manages lifecycle callbacks automatically to: - optimize memory usage - restore UI state - handle multitasking - manage interruptions

Core lifecycle methods: - onCreate() - onStart() - onResume() - onPause() - onStop() - onDestroy()

docs.title: What's the difference between onStart() and onResume()?
docs.text:
beginner android lifecycle callbacks View Answer

onStart(): Called when Activity becomes visible to user. - Window not yet in focus - Activity cannot receive user input - Use for resource allocation needed for UI visibility

onResume(): Called when Activity gains focus and is ready for interaction. - Window is in focus - Can receive user input - Use for animations, camera, location updates

Simple rule: onStart = visible, onResume = interactive.

docs.title: What is savedInstanceState and when is it called?
docs.text:
intermediate android lifecycle state-preservation View Answer

savedInstanceState is a Bundle used to preserve Activity state during predictable destruction (rotation, low memory).

Called in order: 1. onPause() 2. onSaveInstanceState() 3. onStop()

Common use cases: - Save fragment state - Save scroll position - Save form data - Save UI state

Note: NOT called during activity finish() or user back press.

docs.title: What happens during configuration changes (rotation)?
docs.text:
intermediate android lifecycle configuration View Answer

When device is rotated or configuration changes: 1. onPause() → onSaveInstanceState() → onStop() → onDestroy() 2. onCreate() → onStart() → onResume()

The Activity is DESTROYED and RECREATED.

To preserve data: - Store in savedInstanceState Bundle - Use ViewModel (survives config changes) - Use retained fragments - Add android:configChanges to manifest

Best practice: Use ViewModel for non-UI state.

docs.title: How does Android handle process death?
docs.text:
intermediate android lifecycle process-management View Answer

Process death occurs when Android kills app to free memory (no warning, no lifecycle callbacks).

Recovery steps when user returns: 1. OS restarts app process 2. Activity onCreate() called with savedInstanceState 3. App can restore state from Bundle

Without state saving: Data loss, UI reset.

Solutions: - Implement onSaveInstanceState() - Use ViewModel + Room - Persist critical data to disk/database - Use Hilt for dependency injection

docs.title: What is the exact order of lifecycle callbacks?
docs.text:
beginner android lifecycle callbacks View Answer

NORMAL SEQUENCE: onCreate() → onStart() → onResume() → (user interaction) → onPause() → onStop() → onDestroy()

VISIBLE BUT NOT INTERACTIVE: onStart() (no onResume yet - dialog shown)

ANOTHER APP IN FOREGROUND: onPause() → onStop() (but not onDestroy)

BACK TO APP: onStart() → onResume()

DEVICE ROTATION: onPause() → onSaveInstanceState() → onStop() → onDestroy() → onCreate() → onStart() → onResume()
